articles.title: Experts in Canada are testing doorbell cameras' for Polar bears, called Bear-vision, they combine radar and cameras to …
articles.summary: Researchers are testing Bear-vision cameras to warn communities in Canada about approaching polar bears.
articles.body: Researchers are testing Bear-vision cameras to warn communities in Canada about approaching polar bears. Conservation charity Polar Bears International is developing Bear-vision, a warning system built on security camera technology that can be paired with shorter-range radar. Its first deployment is planned at Churchill’s waste facility this autumn to help monitor bears and reduce surprise encounters, the organisation’ noted in a blog post.The camera is intended to offer a more affordable, easy-to-use alternative to wide-area radar systems. Researchers will use data gathered at the site to train it to recognise polar bears and send notifications when they appear. The project comes as bears gather along Hudson Bay, waiting for sea ice to return so they can hunt seals, while communities work to keep people and wildlife safely apart.How will Bear-vision workBear-vision builds on the organisation’s earlier Bear-dar detection work. While Bear-dar monitors wider areas using radar, the new system uses smart security camera technology and can incorporate shorter-range radar.​Polar Bears International compares the intended function to a doorbell camera that alerts residents when a polar bear is outside. The Churchill deployment will help researchers gather the information needed to train the notification system.Why is Churchill’s waste facility the first locationChurchill began working with Polar Bears International to keep bears out of its dump after a fire destroyed its waste facilities. Garbage can attract bears looking for food, creating risks for both the animals and people nearby.The response includes new electric fences, Bear-dar and Bear-vision monitoring, and a visit by a Churchill delegation to a waste management facility in Greenland. The camera trial is part of a broader effort to manage the site, not replace physical barriers or other measures.Why are bears spending longer near communitiesPolar Bears International says climate-driven sea ice loss leaves bears waiting on land about a month longer than their grandparents did. The ice-free period around Hudson Bay now lasts three to four weeks longer than in the 1980s, placing additional strain on their stored fat reserves.The organisation says these longer periods ashore make coexistence measures increasingly important. Its Polar Bear Week, running November 1–7, coincides with the seasonal gathering near Churchill.What other tools are researchers testingPolar Bears International and Brigham Young University are also working with Churchill’s Polar Bear Alert Program to test drones as an affordable, non-lethal way to move bears away from communities. That separate deterrent project includes ultrasonic sound, conductive materials and a new odour-based bear spray formula.​“It’s not easy to live with large predators as your neighbours, so we’re investing in coexistence approaches, especially as we see climate change causing more human-bear encounters. By developing and field-testing innovative, non-lethal deterrents like drones and detection tech like Bear-vision, we’re hoping to expand the variety of safe, effective, and affordable coexistence tools available to communities,” said Geoff York, Polar Bears International’s vice president of science and policy.​​You use AI every day. articles.title: Cinco bombeiros se uniram para conseguir carregar sucuri de até 80 kg  | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo o tenente Fábio Mesquita, o réptil media 4,5 metros e pesava até 80 quilos. A sucuri estava prestes a comer um cachorro quando foi capturada pelos bombeiros.
articles.summary: Segundo o tenente Fábio Mesquita, o réptil media 4,5 metros e pesava até 80 quilos. A sucuri estava prestes a comer um cachorro quando foi capturada pelos bombeiros.
articles.body:
Cinco bombeiros se uniram para carregar a sucuri gigante que foi capturada em uma residência em Caldas Novas, no sul de Goiás. Segundo o tenente Fábio Mesquita, o réptil media 4,5 metros e pesava até 80 quilos. A sucuri estava prestes a comer um cachorro quando foi capturada pelos bombeiros.

O episídio aconteceu nesta quarta-feira (4). O Corpo de Bombeiros informou que a presença da sucuri deixou os moradores preocupados devido a presença de crianças e animais domésticos. Foi o tutor do cachorro atacado pela serpente que acionou os bombeiros.

O tenente Fábio relatou que, dias antes da captura, a sucuri já havia comido outros animais como galinhas e gatos. "Ela pegou o cachorro, mas os moradores mexeram com ela e ela o soltou", contou.

Apesar de não ter comido o cachorro, a sucuri matou o animal doméstico por asfixia. Como a serpente não havia se alimentado, os bombeiros usaram o cachorro para conseguir capturar o réptil.

Após as manobras para pegar a sucuri, o animal foi retirado da residência forma segura e encaminhado ao Centro de Triagem e Reabilitação de Animais Silvestres (Cetras) para receber os cuidados necessários.

A serpente foi capturada e levada ao Centro de Triagem e Reabilitação de Animais Silvestres pelo Corpo de Bombeiros — Foto: Divulgação/Corpo de Bombeiros

De acordo com o tenente, a sucuri é a terceira maior que já capturou nos 20 anos em que trabalha em Caldas Novas. Ao g1 , o biólogo Edson Abrão explicou que a sucuri é uma espécie de serptente que não possui veneno, mas tem uma musculatura muito forte.

"Então, ela não injeta peçonha quando morde uma pessoa. Mas ela mata animais por constrição, ela é um animal muito forte. Na América do Sul, ela é a serpente que mais tem força no corpo, e se alimenta de qualquer animal”, explicou o biólogo.

🔍 A constrição é uma forma de predação em que a serpente envolve o corpo da presa e usa a força muscular para imobilizá-la. A alimentação da sucuri pode incluir mamíferos, peixes, jacarés e até outras serpentes.

Ainda segundo o biólogo, a sucuri é uma espécie semiaquática e pode ter se aproximado da residência em busca de abrigo ou alimento. Apesar do susto que causa, Abrão esclareceu que a presença de um animal adulto e desse porte na região pode indicar que o ambiente está em equilíbrio ecológico.

Esse equilíbrio ocorre porque a sucuri ocupa uma posição importante na cadeia alimentar, pois controla as populações de outras espécies. Abrão ressaltou que animais silvestres não devem ser mortos quando aparecem em áreas residenciais.

Sucuri-amarela gigante foi capturada e levada ao Centro de Triagem e Reabilitação de Animais Silvestres pelo Corpo de Bombeiros — Foto: Divulgação/CBMGO

articles.title: IBGE abre 1.176 vagas em Pernambuco para trabalhar no Censo | G1
articles.standfirst: Inscrições podem ser feitas até 25 de novembro. Salário oferecido é de R$ 1.741, além de benefícios e pagamento por produtividade.
articles.summary: Inscrições podem ser feitas até 25 de novembro. Salário oferecido é de R$ 1.741, além de benefícios e pagamento por produtividade.
articles.body:
O Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística ( IBGE ) abriu, nesta sexta-feira (6), as inscrições para preencher 1.176 vagas temporárias para trabalhar no 12º Censo Agropecuário, Florestal e Aquícola em Pernambuco. É possível se inscrever até o dia 25 de novembro na internet . Ao todo, a seleção oferece 27 mil vagas em todo o Brasil ( veja vídeo acima ).

A taxa de inscrição é de R$ 70. Para a vaga de recenseador, o IBGE exige ensino fundamental completo. O processo seletivo conta com prova objetiva, a ser aplicada no dia 31 de janeiro de 2027, das 13h às 17h, de acordo com o edital, disponível na internet .

As vagas estão distribuídas por municípios de todo o estado. O salário oferecido é de R$ 1.741, além de pagamento por produtividade, calculado de acordo com o número de unidades visitadas e de questionários aplicados.

Os selecionados também terão direito a benefícios como auxílio-alimentação de R$ 1.192, auxílio pré-escolar, 13º salário proporcional, férias proporcionais e auxílio para custear os deslocamentos.

Segundo o IBGE, os profissionais selecionados serão responsáveis por:

atualizar mapas e endereços das áreas de trabalho;

registrar informações nos dispositivos eletrônicos de coleta;

participar de treinamentos e atividades de acompanhamento da operação censitária.

Ainda de acordo com o instituto, a coleta do censo vai produzir informações sobre a realidade do campo brasileiro e subsidiar políticas públicas, pesquisas e decisões voltadas ao desenvolvimento dos setores agropecuário, florestal e aquícola.

articles.title: Carcará em Rio Preto: ave 'se exibe' para câmera de TV TEM | G1
articles.standfirst: Ave, comum na região, 'se exibiu' para a câmera da torre da TV TEM por alguns minutos e as poses foram gravadas pela central técnica da emissora.
articles.summary: O carcará em São José do Rio Preto se aproximou da lente da torre da TV TEM, deixando a paisagem em segundo plano enquanto exibia seu olhar atento para a câmera.
articles.body:
Um carcará se "exibe" ao pousar em frente a uma das câmeras na torre da TV TEM , em São José do Rio Preto (SP), na manhã desta sexta-feira (6). A ave se aproximou da lente e praticamente tomou conta da imagem, deixando em segundo plano a paisagem da cidade.

Com o bico pertinho da câmera e o olhar “atento”, a ave parece ter ficado curiosa com o equipamento. O flagrante das poses rendeu uma imagem inusitada e foi gravado pela central técnica da emissora. Assista acima.

Carcará pousa em frente à câmera da TV TEM em Rio Preto (SP) — Foto: Reprodução/TV TEM

Conhecido por ser uma ave de rapina bastante comum em áreas abertas e ambientes urbanos, o carcará também costuma ser visto em estradas, campos e até perto de construções.

Esta não foi a primeira vez que um carcará pousou no local. Em 2023, a ave conseguiu os minutos de fama ao desfilar em frente à câmera.

articles.title: Bolsonaro e Wal do Açaí: Justiça rejeita ação de funcionária fantasma | G1
articles.standfirst: Juiz entendeu que não há 'prova cabal de nomeação fictícia' e que pequeno comércio de açaí não era, por si só, incompatível com as atribuições de assessora de Bolsonaro. MP pode recorrer.
articles.summary: Bolsonaro e Wal do Açaí tiveram ação de improbidade rejeitada pela Justiça Federal, que não viu provas de nomeação fictícia em gabinete na Câmara dos Deputados.
articles.body:
A Justiça Federal do Distrito Federal rejeitou, nesta quinta-feira (5), uma ação de improbidade administrativa contra o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro e Walderice Santos da Conceição, conhecida como Wal do Açaí , por atuação dela como funcionária fantasma na Câmara dos Deputados .

O juiz Rodrigo de Godoy Mendes, da 6ª Vara Federal Cível do DF, afirmou que a extinção da ação proposta pelo Ministério Público Federal (MPF) é medida que se impõe, uma vez que ficou demonstrado que Wal do Açaí atuava como interlocutora entre moradores da Vila Histórica de Mambucaba, em Angra dos Reis (RJ), e o gabinete de Bolsonaro na Câmara .

Segundo o magistrado, “a exploração do pequeno comércio de açaí (‘Wal Açaí’), instalado na parte frontal de terreno familiar, não se mostra incompatível com as atribuições de assessoria parlamentar descentralizada, que não impunham exclusividade plena, funcionando, ao revés, como espaço aberto de circulação de pessoas da pequena comunidade litorânea”.

Mendes disse ainda que “eventuais deficiências na comprovação formal de rotina de 40 horas semanais em formulários de frequência atestam desorganização administrativa ou inabilidade no acompanhamento do trabalho externo, mas não autorizam a ilação de que a nomeação foi fraudulenta”.

O juiz ressaltou que as regras da Câmara permitem que secretários parlamentares exerçam atividades nos estados de representação dos deputados, sem a necessidade de permanecer fisicamente em Brasília .

O MPF pode recorrer da decisão . A ação de improbidade foi proposta pelo Ministério Público Federal em março de 2022. Para os procuradores, entre fevereiro de 2012 e agosto de 2018, Walderice e seu companheiro, Edenilson Nogueira Garcia, prestavam serviços de natureza particular para Bolsonaro, especialmente nos cuidados com a casa e com os cachorros do ex-presidente na Vila Histórica de Mambucaba (RJ).

Ela teria recebido salários da Câmara dos Deputados sem exercer efetivamente as funções do cargo . Por isso, o MPF pediu o ressarcimento de R$ 280.273,44 , valor correspondente ao prejuízo causado aos cofres públicos.

O MPF aponta que o então deputado federal tinha pleno conhecimento de que Walderice não prestava os serviços correspondentes ao cargo e, mesmo assim, atestava falsamente a frequência dela ao trabalho em seu gabinete para comprovar o cumprimento da jornada laboral exigida pela Câmara dos Deputados, de 40 horas semanais, e, assim, possibilitar o pagamento dos salários.

Segundo a ação, a análise das contas bancárias de Walderice revelou uma movimentação atípica : 83,77% da remuneração recebida no período foi sacada em espécie. Em alguns anos, esse percentual superou 95% dos rendimentos recebidos.

Wal do Açaí em foto com o presidente e o filho dele, o vereador Carlos Bolsonaro — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Na decisão, o juiz afirmou que os saques em espécie não comprovaram desvio de recursos ou enriquecimento ilícito . Segundo ele, também é preciso considerar que a Vila Histórica de Mambucaba apresentava limitações de acesso a serviços bancários.

“Não há nos autos demonstração de repasse de valores da servidora ao corréu [Bolsonaro], apropriação indevida ou qualquer partilha ilícita de remuneração. O que se observa é o mero saque em espécie da remuneração percebida para atendimento de necessidades rotineiras de subsistência em comunidade desprovida de estrutura bancária presencial”, escreveu.

Na avaliação do juiz, com base nos depoimentos e nas provas juntados ao processo, ficou comprovado que Wal do Açaí “exercia atividades de auxílio e intermediação política no município de sua residência, amparada pelas normas infralegais da Câmara dos Deputados”. Portanto, “a improcedência do pedido de condenação por atos de improbidade administrativa é medida que se impõe”.

“Inexistindo prova cabal de nomeação fictícia, de desvio de função para afazeres domésticos, de locupletamento ilícito e de lesão efetiva aos cofres públicos, e restando ausente a demonstração de dolo específico qualificado e desonestidade, a improcedência integral dos pedidos formulados na inicial é medida que se impõe”, concluiu Mendes.

articles.title: Justiça dos EUA bloqueia obras de Arco do Triunfo de Trump | G1
articles.standfirst: Juíza federal Tanya Chutkan vetou início das obras durante 14 dias. Medida ocorreu após Comissão Nacional de Planejamento da Capital (CNPC) ter aprovado construção.
articles.summary: Juíza federal Tanya Chutkan vetou início das obras durante 14 dias. Medida ocorreu após Comissão Nacional de Planejamento da Capital (CNPC) ter aprovado construção.
articles.body:
Trump quer construir um arco de 76 metros em Washington — Foto: Comissão das Belas Artes

Uma juíza federal dos Estados Unidos bloqueou na noite de quinta-feira (5) o gigantesco projeto de Arco do Triunfo promovido pelo presidente Donald Trump , o que coloca em dúvida o futuro da obra, poucas horas após uma comissão pública ter aprovado o projeto.

A juíza federal distrital Tanya Chutkan, que supervisiona o caso, determinou que o governo Trump não pode iniciar a construção do monumento por duas semanas, enquanto o tribunal avalia as contestações sobre sua legalidade.

A Comissão Nacional de Planejamento da Capital (NCPC) aprovou na quinta-feira, por 8 votos a 4, o projeto, apesar de ter ouvido durante horas os depoimentos de dezenas de opositores que questionavam sua validade e finalidade.

A principal queixa é a localização da estrutura de 76 metros de altura: ao lado do venerado Cemitério Nacional de Arlington, local onde foram enterrados centenas de milhares de militares americanos.

O gigantesco monumento seria significativamente maior que o Arco do Triunfo de Paris, no qual é inspirado. Também seria maior que o Memorial Lincoln, do outro lado do rio Potomac.

Os quatro comissários que votaram contra o projeto solicitaram o adiamento da decisão, apontando preocupações jurídicas, a falta de uma verba aprovada pelo Congresso para financiar o projeto e dúvidas sobre as afirmações do secretário de Defesa, Pete Hegseth, sobre o uso militar do arco.

Mas a maioria do painel, controlado por aliados de Trump, votou contra o adiamento e o governo afirmou que seu objetivo era iniciar as obras imediatamente.

A decisão de Chutkan está de acordo com a opinião de veteranos militares e dos procuradores-gerais de Washington e da Virgínia, que haviam apresentado uma ação para impedir a construção do arco.

Desde seu retorno à Casa Branca em janeiro de 2025, Trump estimula projetos de construção e reformas para impor sua marca em Washington.

Entre as obras mais famosas está um salão de baile na Casa Branca, para o qual o magnata republicano mandou demolir uma ala inteira da mansão presidencial.

A Suprema Corte decidiu, por fim, que o autor da ação apresentada para interromper o projeto não tinha legitimidade.

Outra obra importante é a reforma do espelho d'água no National Mall. Trump também propôs reformar o East Potomac Golf Links, um histórico campo de golfe de Washington, derrubando centenas de árvores, mas um juiz interrompeu o projeto.

Na quinta-feira, Trump assinou um texto que declarou o Salão Oval da Casa Branca um "monumento histórico".

articles.title: Como funcionava esquema de agiotagem que tomou imóveis em Campinas | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo o Ministério Público, grupo cobrava juros abusivos, usava contratos com imóveis como garantia e chegava a recusar pagamentos para tomar propriedades.
articles.summary: Investigação da Operação Shylock revela como esquema de agiotagem em Campinas usava juros abusivos e bloqueio de pagamentos para tomar 18 imóveis das vítimas.
articles.body:
O grupo suspeito de agiotagem que deixou pelo menos 18 pessoas sem imóveis em Campinas (SP) chegava a recusar pagamentos das vítimas para impedir que elas quitassem as dívidas e, assim, tomar suas propriedades. A estratégia foi detalhada pelo Ministério Público de São Paulo (MP-SP) nesta sexta-feira (6), após a Operação Shylock, que prendeu sete investigados.

Segundo o MP, os suspeitos ofereciam empréstimos a pessoas com dificuldades para conseguir crédito em bancos e exigiam imóveis como garantia. Os contratos previam juros menores do que os efetivamente cobrados e, em alguns casos, os pagamentos já realizados eram desconsiderados para aumentar artificialmente as dívidas.

Em um dos casos investigados, uma vítima pagou parcelas durante mais de dois anos, embora o contrato assinado previsse vencimento em apenas três meses . Quando os suspeitos deixaram de reconhecer os pagamentos, passaram a cobrar juros e multas acumulados desde o prazo original, elevando a dívida a um valor que a vítima não tinha condições de pagar.

Ao todo, pelo menos 62 pessoas foram identificadas como vítimas do esquema, segundo o Ministério Público.

De acordo com o Grupo de Atuação Especial de Combate ao Crime Organizado (Gaeco), o grupo tinha uma estrutura organizada, com integrantes responsáveis por encontrar pessoas interessadas em empréstimos, conceder o dinheiro, preparar os contratos e receber os pagamentos.

O esquema funcionava da seguinte maneira:

Busca pelas vítimas: intermediários procuravam pessoas que precisavam de dinheiro, especialmente aquelas com dificuldades para conseguir empréstimos bancários. Para participar, era necessário ter um imóvel em seu nome.

Oferta do empréstimo: os intermediários colocavam essas pessoas em contato com os chamados investidores, responsáveis por emprestar o dinheiro.

Assinatura do contrato: os documentos eram formalizados em cartório, com juros de 1% ao mês e vencimento em dois ou três meses, por exemplo. No entanto, os acordos verbais previam juros de aproximadamente 3% ao mês e pagamentos por períodos maiores.

Pagamento das parcelas: as vítimas recebiam boletos ou chaves PIX para pagar as dívidas. Em alguns casos, o dinheiro era enviado a empresas ou pessoas que não apareciam nos contratos como responsáveis pelos empréstimos.

Cobrança de uma dívida maior: depois de determinado período, os suspeitos passavam a recusar pagamentos ou alegar que parcelas anteriores não haviam sido pagas corretamente. Com isso, cobravam novamente os valores, acrescidos de juros e multas .

Perda do imóvel: quando a dívida atingia um valor que a vítima não conseguia pagar, o grupo acionava a garantia prevista no contrato . As propriedades podiam ser levadas a leilão ou transferidas aos próprios credores.

Segundo o MP, os contratos eram feitos com um mecanismo chamado alienação fiduciária , que permite usar um imóvel como garantia de uma dívida. Se o pagamento não for realizado, a propriedade pode ser tomada pelo credor, desde que sejam cumpridas as condições previstas em lei.

No esquema investigado, porém, os suspeitos teriam usado esse mecanismo para tomar os imóveis mesmo quando as vítimas tentavam continuar pagando .

Durante a coletiva de imprensa, o promotor Rafael Salzedas Arbach, do Gaeco de Campinas, explicou que os contratos tinham condições diferentes daquelas combinadas verbalmente com as vítimas.

"No conteúdo ele parecia um contrato lícito, que previa um vencimento de curto período, de dois ou três meses, no máximo, com juros de 1% ao mês. Mas, na verdade, era um contrato sem data definida com pagamento mais ou menos de 3% ao mês de juros", afirmou.

Como o grupo impedia as vítimas de pagar?

Policiais do Baep em frente a cartório de Campinas (SP) durante cumprimento de mandado da Operação Shylock — Foto: Júnia Vasconcelos/EPTV

Uma das principais estratégias identificadas pelo MP era dificultar o pagamento das parcelas , mesmo quando a pessoa tinha condições de continuar quitando a dívida.

Segundo os investigadores, o grupo usava três empresas para emitir boletos e receber dinheiro. Também indicava chaves PIX de terceiros, incluindo pessoas que não tinham relação aparente com os empréstimos.

Depois, os suspeitos alegavam que os pagamentos não eram válidos , pois o dinheiro não havia sido transferido diretamente para quem constava como credor no contrato.

"Em outros casos, a pessoa estava pagando e em determinado momento eles diziam: 'Agora a gente não vai mais receber'. Como o pagamento era feito por meio de boletos ou chaves PIX aleatórias, eles falavam: 'A gente não reconhece o pagamento, porque ele não caiu na conta de nenhuma das pessoas que fez o empréstimo para você'", detalhou o promotor.

A partir daí, o grupo passava a cobrar novamente valores já pagos, além de juros e multas acumulados desde o vencimento original do contrato.

Como os documentos previam prazos curtos, os suspeitos conseguiam alegar que a dívida estava vencida havia muito tempo, mesmo quando as vítimas continuavam pagando as parcelas conforme os acordos verbais.

Segundo Arbach, a possibilidade de perder o imóvel também funcionava como forma de pressão, sem que o grupo precisasse recorrer a ameaças físicas.

"Quando a gente pensa em uma agiota normal, ele vai quebrar sua perna, vai bater em você, vai ameaçar sua família. E aqui não. Eles estão com a casa onde a pessoa mora. Eles podem pegar a qualquer momento, não precisam chegar a esse ponto. A estrutura é mais sofisticada do que isso", disse o promotor.

Os imóveis envolvidos eram de médio e alto padrão. A investigação também identificou casos em que as propriedades teriam sido avaliadas abaixo do valor real nos contratos, aumentando o prejuízo das vítimas.

Qual era o papel do funcionário de cartório?

Entre os presos na operação está um escrevente do 4º Cartório de Notas de Campinas. Segundo o Ministério Público, ele ajudava a dar aparência de legalidade aos contratos utilizados pelo grupo .

Arbach afirmou que o funcionário teria facilitado a formalização de documentos cujas condições não correspondiam aos acordos feitos entre as partes.

O MP também suspeita que ele recebia valores extras para dar andamento aos negócios.

Em nota divulgada após a operação, o cartório afirmou que não é investigado e não tem envolvimento com os fatos apurados . Segundo o estabelecimento, a investigação envolve exclusivamente o funcionário, por fatos ainda desconhecidos e sem relação com os serviços prestados.

A defesa do escrevente, representada pelo escritório Alex Lúcio Advogados, informou que solicitou acesso aos documentos da investigação, que tramita sob sigilo, e que só vai se manifestar depois de analisar os elementos disponibilizados.

Operação Shylock resultou na prisão de sete pessoas e apreensão de 10 armas em Campinas (SP) — Foto: BAEP/Divulgação

Além das prisões, a Justiça determinou o bloqueio de bens e recursos financeiros dos investigados, incluindo medidas para proteger imóveis vinculados a contratos ainda ativos.

O objetivo é impedir que outras vítimas percam as propriedades enquanto as investigações continuam.

O grupo é investigado por crimes como agiotagem, extorsão, lavagem de dinheiro, organização criminosa e falsidade ideológica .

Segundo o Gaeco, o contrato mais antigo identificado até agora é de 2019 . A investigação começou depois que uma das vítimas procurou o Ministério Público e apresentou documentos sobre o caso.

Os investigadores acreditam que outras pessoas também possam ter sido prejudicadas. Denúncias podem ser feitas pelo sistema de Atendimento ao Cidadão.

articles.title: 'He's done a fantastic job': Trump backs Hegseth amid growing calls for his removal
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has defended secretary of war Pete Hegseth amid calls for his resignation and impeachment, praising his work and backing the US
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has defended secretary of war Pete Hegseth amid calls for his resignation and impeachment, praising his work and backing the US military operations in Iran and Venezuela.When asked whether he was considering changes to his administration, particularly at the Pentagon, Trump dismissed criticism of Hegseth and said the defence chief had performed "a fantastic job"."United States Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, has done a fantastic job. Now, it's got some interesting things. You know, we had more generals than we did in World War II. Everybody was a four-star general. I never saw anything like it. And many of those people were woke. I don't like a woke general, and so he probably has opposition. I think he's done a fantastic job," Trump said.The president also sought to defend his administration's military record, citing operations involving Venezuela and Iran as evidence of the Pentagon's performance. He claimed the operation in Venezuela was completed in 48 minutes without any American fatalities, describing it as one of the greatest attacks witnessed.He also claimed Iran could take 25 to 30 years to recover from the military campaign, while keeping open the possibility of further strikes.The pressure on Hegseth comes in the aftermath of the November 3 midterm elections, in which Republican losses are expected to strengthen Democratic oversight of the Trump administration.Hegseth faces impeachment pressureTrump's public endorsement comes as Hegseth faces growing scrutiny from lawmakers over the administration's handling of the Iran conflict, with members of Congress calling for his removal.Republican Congressman Thomas Massie said on November 4 that he would not reintroduce impeachment articles against Hegseth if the Pentagon chief resigned."There is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns," Massie said in a post on X, according to CNN.Democratic Congressman Jason Crow has also demanded Hegseth's removal, alleging that his leadership has put American military personnel at greater risk.Meanwhile, Hegseth posted a video on X Thursday defending the war against Iran.Hegseth described the Iran war as a “courageous and historic effort” that he said would “ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon.” He dismissed the impeachment articles against him as a “sham,” accusing political opponents of trying to destroy their rivals.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2026, 20 scientists, artists and writers received $800,000 each through the MacArthur 'genius' grants; here is what their work aims to change
articles.summary: The MacArthur Foundation has named 20 fellows whose work spans climate science, history, philosophy, chemistry, poetry, dance and jazz.
articles.body: The MacArthur Foundation has named 20 fellows whose work spans climate science, history, philosophy, chemistry, poetry, dance and jazz. The prize rewards people rather than projects, and nobody can apply for it. Nominations feed a selection process lasting years, and many recipients say they were stunned by the news. The recognition often opens further doors. Reading the full class together shows recurring concerns: damage to the climate and the environment, the memory of violence and injustice, hidden or erased communities, and technology that could make medicine, farming and materials safer and more efficient.Researchers aim to bring communities into clean energy, forecast polar ice and predict harvestsAccording to The Associated Press, Holly Jean Buck, a sociologist at the University at Buffalo, studies the part local communities play in limiting climate change and moving towards clean energy. Marika Holland, a climate scientist based in Boulder, Colorado, helps predict changes in ice cover and works out how polar climate change affects marine ecosystems.Kaiyu Guan, an environmental scientist at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, uses data and machine learning to help farmers predict and optimise their crop yields.Scholars revisit history to explain racial wealth gaps, Indigenous nationhood and federal powerEllora Derenoncourt, a labour economist at Princeton University, investigates where racial wealth disparities in the United States came from and which policies could narrow the gap. Her Princeton colleague Elizabeth Ellis, a historian, is correcting the colonial record to highlight the different ideas of nationhood held by Indigenous tribes and the strategies Native Americans used to resist European settlement.Ariel Ron, a historian at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, examines how agriculture in the northern states influenced economic growth and the expansion of federal power in nineteenth-century America.Memory, forgiveness and loss: A philosopher, a forensic anthropologist, a novelist and a poetFelipe De Brigard, a philosopher at Duke University, applies cognitive science to the link between memory and forgiveness, including among victims of political violence in his home country of Colombia. Kate Spradley, a forensic anthropologist at Texas State University, works to identify migrants who died along the Texas-Mexico border and to repatriate their remains. Her Operation Identification initiative also tackles the complications that make this work so difficult.Maaza Mengiste, a fiction writer at Wesleyan University, uses historically informed novels to show the human cost of political conflict. Layli Long Soldier, a poet in Santa Fe, reworks historical texts to underline the erasure of Native Americans and pairs her writing with visual art.Dance, sound, murals and jazz, artists reimagine whose stories are told and how they are heardTrajal Harrell, a choreographer and dancer based in Zurich, merges dance traditions into an imagined archive that dissolves the barriers between styles. Christine Sun Kim, an artist in Berlin, conveys the experiences of deaf people and finds new ways to understand sound through drawings, large-scale murals, video and interactive works.Rodney McMillian, an artist at the University of California, Los Angeles, moves between sculpture, painting, video and performance to explore how history and socioeconomic conditions shape belonging in the American South. Chip Thomas, a public artist in Flagstaff, Arizona, turns neglected spaces, mostly in the Navajo Nation, into public works rooted in community history.Vincent Valdez, who divides his time between Houston and San Antonio, paints historical and contemporary scenes that reflect Latino experiences in the United States. Immanuel Wilkins, a New York alto saxophonist and composer, writes music that often reflects historical narratives of injustice. Bryan Washington, a fiction writer in Tokyo, captures modern relationships in novels including “Memorial” and “Palaver”.Chemistry, physics and nanotechnology: Safer reactions, new materials and better disease treatmentsSong Lin, an organic chemist at Stanford University, develops methods that open routes to safer and more sustainable synthetic organic reactions. Vincenzo Vitelli, a physicist at the University of Chicago, builds theoretical frameworks to describe how matter and materials with unusual properties will behave.Liangfang Zhang, a chemical engineer and bioengineer at the University of California, San Diego, is creating new nanotechnologies to treat and prevent infectious diseases, cancers and immunological disorders.You use AI every day. articles.body: CHENNAI: A 38-year-old man surrendered at Neelankarai police station after stabbing his 33-year-old wife to death during a domestic dispute at their rented house in Palavakkam on Friday morning.The woman suffered 10 stab injuries to her neck and jaw, police said.The deceased, Muthupriya, a BSc graduate from Sivaganga district, married Vivek, a native of Thiruvarur district, five years ago after they met through a matrimonial service.Vivek worked as a driver at a luxury hotel. The couple had a two-and-a-half-year-old daughter, Thiruvenba.The family moved into a rented house in Palavakkam, a month ago. Police said Vivek frequently quarrelled with his wife, accusing her of having deceived him before their marriage.During the fresh altercation, Vivek knocked Muthupriya to the ground and stabbed her repeatedly with a kitchen knife. She died at the spot.After the incident, Vivek took their daughter to his brother Vinoth’s house in Mudichur and left her in his care.He then went to Neelankarai police station and surrendered, informing the police that he had killed his wife. articles.title: In 2018, Denzel Washington helped lead a $5 million effort to rescue playwright August Wilson's deteriorating childhood home in Pittsburgh; it reopened in 2022 as a 6,000-square-foot arts and community centre
articles.summary: Some houses preserve memories, while others hold the beginnings of stories that eventually shape generations.
articles.body: Some houses preserve memories, while others hold the beginnings of stories that eventually shape generations. In Pittsburgh's historic Hill District, a modest childhood home has become a lasting tribute to one of America's most celebrated playwrights, August Wilson. Once deteriorating and at risk of being lost, the property where Wilson spent his formative years has been transformed into a 6,000-square-foot arts and community centre. The restoration, supported by a fundraising campaign led by Hollywood actor Denzel Washington, has given the building a renewed purpose while preserving the surroundings that influenced Wilson's celebrated body of work. Scroll down to read the details.A childhood home saved from decayAccording to Architectural Digest, Washington spearheaded a $5 million fundraising initiative in September 2018 to support the restoration of Wilson's childhood home in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. The Oscar-winning actor, who directed and starred in the 2016 film adaptation of Wilson's play Fences, was among the prominent supporters who helped mobilise resources for the project.Other contributors included Oprah Winfrey, Tyler Perry, Shonda Rhimes, Spike Lee and Samuel L. Jackson, with Winfrey and Perry each contributing $1 million.Wilson, born Frederick August Kittel Jr., lived in the Bedford Avenue property with his mother, Daisy, and five siblings from 1945 to 1958. The neighbourhood, known as the Hill District, would later become an important influence on his writing, providing the cultural and social backdrop for much of his work, the Architectural Digest report adds.However, by the early 2000s, the building had fallen into disrepair. According to the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, Wilson's nephew, Paul Ellis, purchased the property shortly before the playwright's death in 2005, hoping to preserve it. Together with architect Rob Pfaffmann, he established the nonprofit Daisy Wilson Artist Community to oversee its restoration.From a deteriorating building to a cultural destinationThe preservation process involved several years of planning and structural work. The property received Pittsburgh historic landmark status in 2008, followed by emergency stabilisation efforts between 2010 and 2016. It was also added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2013.The $5 million fundraising campaign launched in 2018 enabled the larger restoration to move forward. Although the project was initially expected to finish in 2020, the pandemic caused delays. The restored property eventually reopened in August 2022.The 6,000-square-foot complex brings together the original 1840s house, an upstairs expansion dating to the 1880s and a contemporary addition. The newer section incorporates elevators, ensuring accessibility throughout the building while allowing its historic architectural elements to remain visible.Preserving Wilson's legacy through the artsRather than functioning solely as a conventional museum, August Wilson House was designed as an active cultural and community space. The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reported that Wilson had wanted his childhood home to remain useful, particularly as a place that could support artists and creative expression.The centre includes four studios for artistic programmes, workshops, reading sessions and discussions. Two indoor galleries will showcase rotating exhibitions, while a rooftop terrace provides space for live performances overlooking Pittsburgh's skyline.Outside, a landscaped garden and outdoor theatre offer opportunities for productions of Wilson's celebrated American Century Cycle, a collection of ten plays exploring African-American experiences across different decades of the 20th century.Inside the rooms where the playwright grew upOne of the most significant sections of the restoration is the preserved upstairs apartment where Wilson spent his childhood. The living room, kitchen, and bedrooms have been meticulously restored to match the family's original surroundings.Details include replica wallpaper based on recollections from Wilson's sister, vintage kitchen appliances and photographic displays featuring images of the Hill District. Restoration workers also uncovered personal artefacts, including shoes concealed inside the walls, believed to have been placed there for good luck.The project concludes by honoring the playwright and his neighborhood. With its combination of preserved domestic spaces, contemporary architecture and creative facilities, August Wilson House offers visitors an opportunity to experience the roots of his storytelling while giving future generations of artists a place to develop their own voices.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia, Facebook, and Pittsburgh Post-GazetteYou use AI every day. articles.title: Desert icons collapse as southwestern US gets pummeled with rain and flooding
articles.summary: There are stretches of high desert in northwestern New Mexico where Mother Nature has sculpted otherworldly forms using wind, rain and the passage of time.He...
articles.body:
There are stretches of high desert in northwestern New Mexico where Mother Nature has sculpted otherworldly forms using wind, rain and the passage of time.

Hefty planks of rock defy gravity as they balance atop spindly pedestals of clay, while some columns of sandstone take on the appearance of lace, elaborately eroded by the seasons.

Tour guide Kialo Winters shares this piece of his homeland on the edge of the Ah-Shi-Sle-Pah Wilderness with visitors regularly. On a recent Friday afternoon, the founder of Navajo Tours USA rounded a bend and found one of the area's most famous features had collapsed.

The Alien Throne — or Tsé Bináká Níyol as it's known in his language — was no more. His heart dropped.

"It was surreal," he told The Associated Press. "I had to sort of just pause. A lot of things ran through my head."

The Alien Throne and the nearby King of Wings formation collapsed within weeks of each other, toppled by the very forces of nature that created them.

Back-to-back storms destroy homes and hoodoos

The southwestern U.S. has endured major rounds of storms over recent weeks, with rain falling on ground already soaked from an especially wet fall.

Parts of New Mexico, Colorado, Utah and Arizona have watched rivers crest and floodwaters course through usually dry washes, destroying homes, further saturating the soil and eroding the landscape.

The water is receding and cleanup is underway, but officials estimate the damage could stretch into the hundreds of millions of dollars.

Winters still is concerned for relatives on the Navajo Nation, where many dirt roads became impassable or were washed away altogether by what he described as a series of massive storm fronts.

Experts have estimated that more than 20 trillion gallons (75.7 trillion liters) of rain fell across the Four Corners states and Nevada during late October and early November as tropical moisture was funneled into the region.

Condolences shared after the features collapse

In early October, the demise of the King of Wings began circulating on social media. Visitors documented the large slab of rock on the ground near the mound of clay on which it once stood.

It's not entirely clear when the Alien Throne came down, as poor road conditions kept Winters from visiting for a couple weeks. He had not seen any other posts about the feature's status until he rounded that corner Oct. 30 and saw it in pieces.

Social media posts ranged from those who were thankful they were able to see the formations and immortalize them with photographs to those lamenting that they never had the chance.

Condolences also were sprinkled in with debates about physics and the fragility of natural wonders.

"Gravity. It's not just a good idea … it's the law," one joked.

For Winters and other Native Americans from the region, they're more than just rock formations. They have served as waypoints, guiding ancestors along trade routes for thousands of years, and as connecting threads in stories handed down through generations.

"They are culturally relevant to our identity and our stories," he said, adding that their legacies will be carried on through photographs, illustrations and in the stories people share about their time spent in this stretch of desert.

He called on people to let the sites "rest." So no climbing on what remains, and certainly don't take any pieces home.

It's far off the beaten path down a rutted, washboard dirt road. But it's worth it, said Alan Studt of Parma, Ohio, who made his first visit in 2019 and then again last April as part of a 50-day road trip.

In looking back through his earlier photographs, he could see the formations were weathering. There were new holes forming in the throne and cracks along the wing's base, making it no surprise they would not last forever.

Studt spent hours exploring and photographing the hills and washes during this last trip. He described being drawn in each time he saw a new set of spires in the distance, marveling at the petrified wood along the way and the rainbow of colors in the soils.

"It is really so magical to be out there," he said.

articles.title: In 1944, Canadian Captain W. E. Duggan Gray lost his engraved silver flask in France; fellow soldier James McCorriston kept it and returned it nearly 48 years later
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable story of how a silver flask, lost by Canadian Captain W.E. Duggan Gray in 1944 during WWII, was returned 48 years later by fellow soldier James McCorriston, showcasing the enduring power of memories and connections forged in battle.
articles.body: Some lost things remain lost forever. Others show up when least expected. According to the Royal Canadian Artillery Museum, an engraved silver flask belonging to Canadian captain W.E. Duggan Gray was lost in France in 1944. It ended up with another soldier, James McCorriston, who kept it safe for decades. Finally, in 1992, he returned it, nearly 48 years after it disappeared.A young officer on Juno BeachGray landed on Juno Beach on D-Day, June 6, 1944. He was serving with the 3rd Anti-Tank Regiment, a unit in the 3rd Canadian Division. A Veterans Affairs Canada backgrounder says there were approximately 14,000 Canadians who landed at Juno Beach on June 6, 1944, where they were met with intense enemy fire. The Germans had heavily fortified the coastline with machine guns, mines, and barbed wire. A separate Veterans Affairs Canada web page on the Bény-sur-Mer Canadian War Cemetery states that the 3rd Division and the 2nd Armoured Brigade formed the main Canadian ground force for that day. Gray’s regiment paid dearly for the war. The museum notes one of his batteries had lost 50 percent over 3 days.A wound and a terrible mix-up In 1944, Gray was still fighting in France when a German mortar hit his leg. British soldiers found him and took him to a hospital. Then things went wrong. His unit thought he was dead and sent a telegram to his family saying so. His parents were grief-stricken. The unit corrected the mistake shortly after they found out Gray was alive and recovering. In a 1992 newspaper article, Gray described himself back in 1944 as “young, stupid, and very fatalistic.” He added that he laughed about the mix-up afterwards.How the flask went missingThere was yet another consequence of the false news. Before anyone realised that Gray was alive, his regiment had sent his kit to the divisional headquarters to get rid of it. The kit had his silver flask with the inscription “D.Gray” on it, and it was full of military rum. Once Gray was discovered alive, his regiment went back for his belongings. By that time, however, the rum and the flask had disappeared. The loss was minor compared to the war around it. Gray didn't know that McCorriston, another Canadian soldier, was carrying the flask through the rest of the war.The search that ended at a dinnerMcCorriston kept the flask for decades after the war. With the assistance of the War Graves Commission and Legion Magazine, he traced its owner in 1991. He returned it to Gray in 1992 at the reunion dinner of the 3rd Anti-Tank Regiment. The Vernon Daily News published a story on January 18, 1992, with a headline saying the flask was back after 47 years. McCorriston said that a girl had given him the flask, while Gray believed McCorriston had helped himself to the rum.Why a small object still matters Gray was mentioned twice in dispatches by the Canadian military for service in France and Belgium. Later, he passed his wartime keepsakes to his son. In 2008, his son, Nairne Gray, of Vancouver, donated them to the museum. The collection included the flask, a Second World War helmet, a framed set of medals, discharge papers and one newspaper article. The family donated the items to the museum to keep the legacy of their father, the museum said. A flask is just metal, but this one held an entire story of a wound, a fake death notice and a very long wait. The story shows that behind every great date in history are real people, and little things like this one help keep their stories alive.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Essex Reform councillor branded racist by Labour opposition
articles.summary: Carl Johnson writes that "no foreigner" should be allowed to stand in elections.
articles.body:
A Reform UK councillor has been labelled a "racist" and accused of posting "xenophobic conspiracy theories" by a Labour councillor, after questioning whether migrants and their children should be allowed to stand for elected office.

Essex county councillor Carl Johnson posted a picture of Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood next to London Mayor Sadiq Khan, and wrote "we have been deliberately infiltrated".

Labour county councillor Lee Scordis called on Reform to "expel him immediately".

Johnson and his party have both since defended his right to free speech.

"Open debate and free speech should not be shut down simply because others disagree with a particular viewpoint," said Johnson, speaking to the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS).

Johnson shared the image of the two prominent Labour politicians on Wednesday.

In his accompanying message, he wrote: "We have allowed people who arrived as asylum seekers to settle and then have second generations, gain positions of political power, and then push to change our laws to better reflect their own religion and culture.

"That is unacceptable. No foreigner should ever be allowed to stand for political office in this country."

The Facebook post has since been removed from the page of councillor Carl Johnson and the BBC contacted him for a response.

Both the home secretary and London mayor were born in the UK and are the second generation of migrant families.

Scordis said the Reform councillor had suggested that politicians like Winston Churchill and Rishi Sunak, who had at least one parent born abroad, "could not be elected in any role, let alone prime minister".

A Reform spokesperson said: "[The party] is committed to net-negative migration and will prioritise the needs of the British people.

"Councillor Johnson is entitled to his own personal views."

The Braintree Conservatives said they "strongly oppose these remarks, and the obsession of some Reform politicians openly challenging the identity of Britons born in this country".

Meanwhile, Essex County Council said it was "aware of the social media post by councillor Carl Johnson" but would not comment on whether a complaint had been received.

Johnson told the LDRS: "My concern is that individuals who hold positions of political influence in the UK should always act in the interests of this country and its people.

"There have been well-publicised cases where questions have been raised about political figures advocating positions that appear to place the interests of other countries, cultures or ideologies above those of the United Kingdom."

Six moves Reform has made since taking power in Essex

The home secretary's parents immigrated from Kashmir, and Khan's from Pakistan.

Earlier this year, Mahmood told the BBC that friends and family had recently experienced racist slurs "when they had gone 20 years without hearing those words said to them".

"I think we're living in a more divisive, more polarised world. I think social media has a lot to do with sending hateful, divisive stuff through the algorithms," she said, speaking in January.

Johnson did not refer to them directly in his post, but the image he shared of them included the caption: "One changing our capital city, the other bringing in Islam in the thousands."

The Facebook post, before it was removed, had received 14,000 interactions and more than 3,000 comments.

He is the county councillor for Three Fields and Great Notley, which includes MDP Wethersfield, where hundreds of asylum seekers are accommodated.

The Reform leader of Essex County Council Peter Harris has also been approached for comment.

articles.title: Israel’s President Herzog to name candidate to form government on Sunday
articles.summary: Announcement comes after majority of Israeli lawmakers endorse Eisenkot over Netanyahu.
articles.body:
Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has said he will name a candidate to form the country’s next government by Sunday, after a majority of lawmakers backed opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Herzog made the announcement on Thursday after holding marathon talks with parties elected to the 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset.

Some 67 lawmakers endorsed Eisenkot, a former military chief, while 46 backed Netanyahu.

In televised remarks at the end of the talks, Herzog said that although the “results of the consultations may appear clear”, there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the best chance of assembling a governing coalition.

He said he would hold “personal talks with some of the party leaders” over the Israeli weekend, which runs Friday-Saturday, and make a pick on Sunday.

Israel’s October 27 election left neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot with a clear path to a parliamentary majority, handing Herzog the difficult task of choosing a candidate in a deeply divided country.

Netanyahu’s Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, ⁠but his wider religious-nationalist coalition garnered only 53 in total.

Eisenkot’s alliance of four Jewish-led parties, which spans the political spectrum from centre-left to right, won 48 seats despite polls that had predicted a close race.

Two parties representing Israel’s Palestinian minority won an unprecedented 19 seats.

Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties. Both of those parties nonetheless recommended him, giving him the support of a comfortable majority of lawmakers.

“We want to do things that we did not do in the past in order to remove this criminal government,” Ahmad Tibi, a senior member of the Joint List, which represents an alliance of Arab parties, told The Associated Press news agency.

Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, said his 67 recommendations were the most any candidate had received since 2015, and urged Herzog to give him the mandate “as soon as possible” so he could form a national emergency government.

Separately, Netanyahu suffered a setback on Thursday when United Torah Judaism, one of the two main ultra-Orthodox parties and a longtime ally, declined to recommend any candidate.

The party broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.

Yariv Oppenheimer, a member of the Democrats, a party in Eisenkot’s alliance, told Al Jazeera that he saw “no reason” Herzog would not choose Eisenkot on Sunday.

He said United Torah Judaism had signalled that its support was available for the right price, meaning that a good enough offer from Eisenkot could give him the numbers he needed.

“It’s very clear that Netanyahu doesn’t have a chance to establish a government at all,” he added.

Once nominated by Herzog, the candidate will have 28 days to try to forge a government, with a possible 14-day extension.

Netanyahu will remain prime minister in a caretaker government until a new coalition is formed, or through another election that must be held if no ⁠candidate succeeds.

Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, has seized on an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast doubt on the results, accusing Arab-led parties of stealing the vote.

Critics accuse Netanyahu and his partners of trying to undermine the results, which he denies.

Israel’s Central Election Committee said on ‌Wednesday that the election’s integrity had not been compromised. The head of the committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, has called on Israel’s elected officials to protect public trust rather than shake it.

“This is a real danger. One of the foundations of democracy is the peaceful transfer of power,” Sohlberg ‌told ‌Herzog at his residence on Wednesday. High voter turnout, including among the Arab minority, was a blessing, he said.

Netanyahu’s allies on the far-right, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, have called for the immediate arrest and interrogation of Arab party leaders.

articles.title: India’s only floating post office in Kashmir’s Dal Lake gets longer working hours
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: The Department of Posts today said that it has extended the working hours of the iconic Floating Post Office at Nehru Park in Dal Lake,
articles.body: SRINAGAR: The Department of Posts today said that it has extended the working hours of the iconic Floating Post Office at Nehru Park in Dal Lake, Srinagar, which will now remain operational from 9:00 AM to 9:00 PM.The initiative follows the encouraging public response, the department’s spokesperson said.Chief Postmaster General, Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh, Col. Sagar Hanuman Singh, visited the floating post office today reviewing the facilities. He also interacted with customers, tourists and members of the public to understand their requirements.“Considering the considerable footfall at Nehru Park and the demand for postal services beyond regular office hours, the decision was taken to extend the working hours of the facility,” Singh said, adding that the decision aims to provide greater convenience to customers, tourists and the local population.He said the Department of Posts’ commitment to making postal services more accessible, customer-friendly and responsive to public needs.Officials say that the initiative reflects the Department’s continued efforts to improve service delivery and provide greater flexibility in accessing postal facilities. They said the Floating Post Office is not only an important postal facility but also a distinctive attraction for tourists visiting Kashmir.The extended hours will enable local residents, tourists, houseboat operators and other visitors to access postal services at more convenient times, they added.The story of this post office began in 1953, when a simple postal boat started serving the communities living on Dal Lake making it a vital link between the houseboats and the city. In 2011, it was officially renamed the Floating Post Office, an idea introduced by John Samuel, then Postmaster General of the Jammu and Kashmir Circle.After renovation, the houseboat reopened to the public, drawing interest from both locals and travellers.According to officials, it is India's only floating post office. The office has a unique museum showing rare stamps and postcards portraying the history of the postal service in Jammu and Kashmir. Most of its collection was severely damaged in 2014 devastating floods in the Valley.Stay updated with the latest Srinagar news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Tundu Lissu: Tanzania opposition leader found guilty of incitement but acquitted of treason
articles.summary: The 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, says the charges are politically motivated.
articles.body:
Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.

A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.

But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election.

Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.

The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement.

"By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.

Lissu said he had only been charged with treason, not incitement.

"The offence of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offence that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," Lissu told the court.

He added that he would like to apply for bail as this was possible for incitement, unlike treason.

He has leave to appeal at the Court of Appeal - the country's highest court.

But if the four-year sentence is upheld, it would rule him out of the next elections, due in 2030.

Treason is among Tanzania's most serious offences and can carry the death penalty.

Human rights group Amnesty International described his conviction as a "travesty of justice".

"Tundu Lissu should never have been arrested, let alone prosecuted and convicted," said its regional director for East and Southern Africa, Tigere Chagutah:

President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote - a result the opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded.

Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.

Tundu Lissu - the great survivor of Tanzanian politics

Demands for post-poll justice as Tanzania accused of weaponising counterterrorism laws

WATCH: Tundu Lissu: A Fight Too Far? on BBC Africa Eye's YouTube channel

The Chadema leader was arrested six months before the poll, shortly after launching a campaign demanding changes to the electoral system under the slogan "No Reforms, No Election".

Prosecutors accused him of making statements intended to incite the public to disrupt the election and threaten the government.

They argued that his remarks, which were also circulated online, amounted to treason.

But Lissu, a lawyer who represented himself during the trial, maintained that his comments were part of a legitimate political campaign for constitutional and electoral reform.

He argued that prosecutors had taken his statements out of context and failed to prove that he had committed any crime.

Some of the demands raised by Chadema were:

Electoral commissioners should be independently appointed (not by the president)

Police should allow all parties to campaign free of intimidation

Government-appointed district chiefs should no longer act as returning officers

Party agents should be able to observe counting without harassment

It should be possible to challenge presidential election results in court.

During his time in remand custody at Dar es Salaam's Ukonga Prison, Lissu went on hunger strike twice for brief periods when he said he was not allowed access to his lawyers or relatives. He also complained that guards listened to what should have been private consultations his lawyers.

These allegations have been denied by the prison authorities.

His case has attracted international attention, with rights groups expressing concern about the treatment of opposition politicians and the shrinking space for political dissent in Tanzania.

Last year's election was followed by widespread protests and a violent security crackdown that left at least 500 people dead, according to an official inquiry.

Opposition groups have said the death toll was much higher and demanded an independent investigation.

The government has defended its handling of the unrest and rejected accusations of widespread political repression.

Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her. She has set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.

Lissu has long been one of Tanzania's most outspoken critics of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party, which, along with its predecessor Tanu, has dominated the country's politics since independence.

He first became an MP in 2010, representing a constituency near his birth place in Singida, 320km (200 miles) north-west of the capital, Dodoma.

In September 2017, the Chadema politician narrowly survived an assassination attempt when gunmen sprayed his vehicle with bullets outside his home in Dodoma.

He was shot multiple times and underwent extensive medical treatment abroad.

The attack, whose perpetrators have never been brought to justice, forced him to spend years in exile.

He returned to contest the 2020 presidential election against the late President John Magufuli, but lost in a vote that the opposition alleged was marred by widespread irregularities.

Lissu subsequently returned to exile before coming back to Tanzania in 2023, following President Samia's decision to lift a ban on opposition political rallies.

His return was initially seen as a sign of renewed political openness after years of restrictions under Magufuli, who died in office in 2021.

But relations between the government and the opposition deteriorated as the country approached the 2025 election.

Lissu became Chadema's national chairman in January 2025 and intensified his demands for electoral reforms.

His conviction is likely to deepen concerns about the state of democracy in Tanzania.

Last week, Amnesty accused the government of continuing its crackdown following the election and "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".

The authorities did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.body: Ukraine must adapt to the changing political landscape in the United States and move quickly to secure continued American support, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, stressing the need to strengthen bipartisan backing for Kyiv.According to Reuters, in an interview with Ukrainian television channel TSN broadcast on Thursday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine must adjust its approach to Washington following the US midterm elections, in which Democrats gained control of Congress, and work to strengthen support across party lines."Ukraine has to move forward towards the new political infrastructure in the United States of America," Zelenskyy said."We have to move quickly. This is the No 1 priority," he added.The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptor missiles to Ukraine in a deal estimated at $2.1 billion. However, deliveries are expected only in the early 2030s, leaving Kyiv facing an immediate shortage of interceptors.Zelenskyy also said Ukraine was working to ensure it had enough operational F-16 fighter jets over the next five to six months as it prepares for another winter of Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pope Leo’s Latin America trip will take him above 11,000 feet, weeks after lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: Just over three weeks ago, the most significant visit of Pope Leo’s pontificate looked to be in doubt. The 71-year-old’s lung cancer surgery led some in the Vatican to believe his trip to Latin America would be postponed or its intense schedule adjusted.
articles.body: Just over three weeks ago, the most significant visit of Pope Leo’s pontificate looked to be in doubt. The 71-year-old’s lung cancer surgery led some in the Vatican to believe his trip to Latin America would be postponed or its intense schedule adjusted. But Leo XIV is forging ahead with a grueling 12-day visit, which includes Uruguay, Argentina, and an emotional “homecoming” to Peru, the country where he served as a missionary and bishop for around two decades. He plans to cover a lot of ground – around 19,000 miles – while in Latin America. From November 6 to 17, the pope is scheduled to take 14 flights (including two in a helicopter), give 36 speeches and participate in around 50 events in what is one of the most intense papal trips of recent years. He will also visit Cusco, Peru, which is more than 11,000 feet above sea-level and where there is 35% less oxygen per breath. During the whole trip, he’ll travel to 10 cities, preside at large open-air Masses and vigils and meet with political leaders. The trip, especially Cusco’s altitude, has raised questions about his health and the precautions being taken while there. It has also shone a light on a region that has profoundly shaped him and set his path to the papacy. A medical team will be on hand The pontiff had surgery last month to remove a third of his right lung after a small growth was discovered during routine checks, which was later confirmed as cancer. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said afterward that there were “no clinical reasons why this visit should not take place,” and doctors have said he does not need further treatment. Vatican officials told reporters that Pope Leo will have a medical team available to him for the trip but stressed that no special measures are being taken. “We’re speaking of a 71-year-old person in good health,” the Vatican spokesman said ahead of the visit. He explained the pope will travel with the “ordinary medical assistance,” including doctors, nurses and an ambulance, which usually travels with the pope’s convoy. But the spokesman said he wasn’t going into too much detail as the pope does not have a “permanent condition.” And if the Vatican medical team needs any help, one of the journalists traveling with the pope is also a doctor. Montse Alvarado, the new head of Vatican Communications, told journalists on Tuesday that the pope’s “stamina is fantastic,” and that “he’ll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen.” Dr. Matthew Triplette, a pulmonologist from the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in Seattle, told CNN the risk of a medical emergency during the trip is “low” but that this could include “either a collapsed lung or blood clots.” Triplette said the pope may be advised to “take low-dose blood thinners or use exercises or compression devices” to lower the possibility of blood clots in his legs when flying, which could cause major issues if they spread to the lungs. He added that the pope may feel more fatigue with exertion, particularly because there is less oxygen available at altitude. Pope Leo personally pushed ahead with the visit In the aftermath of his surgery, many speculated that the trip would be canceled. “I must confess that, until just a few days ago, I was among the few who had serious doubts about whether this trip could even take place,” Guzmán Carriquiry, a Uruguayan former Vatican official who worked on Latin American issues for nearly 50 years in the church’s central administration, told reporters on Tuesday. But he also pointed out that the pope’s health team gave him the green light. “This suggests that his doctors believe the pope possesses a robust physical constitution; it also serves as a testament to the pope’s ardent desire and determination to go out and meet our people,” he said. But Carriquiry noted that he would have removed Cusco from the agenda if he had organized the trip. While Leo XIV is known for his gentle, low-key style, he is determined. Answering a question from CNN, Alvarado said the pope “personally confirmed this trip with no changes,” and that he was looking forward to returning to Latin America. The continent, and Peru in particular, is close to his heart, and Alvarado said the pope would speak off the cuff frequently in Spanish, a language he is fluent in. “He’s going on this trip very simply because he wants to go,” is how Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican foreign minister, put it at an event in Rome at the end of last month. Peru is at the heart of the trip The Peruvian part of the trip will be emotional, as Leo arrives there “as an adopted brother, adopted by the Peruvian people,” said Carriquiry. The pope, who remains a Peruvian citizen, had three stints in Peru, having first arrived there in his 30s. He also served as Bishop of Chiclayo in the northwest part of the country from 2015 to 2023. The pope will return to Chiclayo during the trip and is expected to receive a rapturous welcome. Leo is remembered fondly in the city, where he was considered a hands-on bishop who was known to travel across his diocese on horseback. “The pope spent many years living amongst the simple, poor and devout people of rural Latin America in northern Peru, as a missionary and a pastor,” Carriquiry, who is the former secretary of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, said. Leo is expected to draw huge crowds when he’s there, with estimates of around 1.2 million people expected to attend his final Mass of the trip at Las Palmas Airbase in Lima. He is also expected to draw huge crowds in Argentina, where more than a million people are expected to attend his Mass in Buenos Aires. The unfinished business of his predecessor in Argentina The late Pope Francis, the first Argentine pontiff, never made a visit to his home country, so Leo’s visit is one that is generating intense interest. Francis never gave a clear reason as to why he didn’t visit Argentina. Carriquiry, a close friend of the late pope, said it “remains an enigma.” Leo XIV’s visit will underline his plans to continue the reforms of his predecessor, but with his own distinctive style. The pope’s visit comes at a time when Argentine President Javier Milei’s “chainsaw” austerity measures have led to welfare spending cuts. Milei has also equated state-led social justice programs with communism. Pope Leo, in contrast, has made the church’s social teaching and concern for the marginalized a central concern of his papacy. His itinerary includes a visit to a federal prison in Buenos Aires and a stop at a care center for people with intellectual and physical disabilities in Claypole which has been affected by the Milei cuts. Both Milei and Peru’s President Keiko Fujimori are notable figures in Latin America’s right-wing surge. They also enjoy support from the Trump administration, which Leo has publicly disagreed with — particularly on migration issues. A missionary pope in a continent that shaped him Leo XIV would not have been elected pope had he not been sent to Peru as a young Augustinian missionary. His time in Latin America put him on a path to be spotted by Pope Francis. It was Francis who appointed the then-Rev. Robert Prevost as bishop in Chiclayo before later bringing him to Rome and naming him a cardinal. All of this set him up as a candidate in the 2025 conclave. While Leo is the first pope from the United States and grew up in Chicago, his experience in Latin America has profoundly influenced his outlook. In Peru, he served in the birthplace of liberation theology, a movement focused on social and political action to help the poor and oppressed. As a bishop, he was known for organizing practical assistance for those affected by floods or in need of medical equipment during the Covid-19 pandemic. He served in a church in Peru which emphasized an inclusive model, giving greater roles to those not ordained as priests and bishops, including women. Leo’s time in Peru also saw him exposed to the fallout of the clerical abuse crisis, including a major scandal involving a powerful Catholic group. The Vatican says the pope will have two meetings with abuse survivors during his trip, one in Argentina and another in Peru. South America remains the continent with the largest Catholic population, although recent years has seen a decline in numbers, and the rise of evangelical churches. In Uruguay, the pope will be in the continent’s most secularized country. Whatever the health challenges, Pope Leo is determined to carry out the most important foreign mission of his pontificate so far: a return to the country that adopted him, and to the region that helped shape the man who would become pope.
