articles.title: Oil-rich UAE makes massive AI bet as Sam Altman unveils ambitious plan to transform energy industry
articles.summary: OpenAI's Sam Altman named energy as his biggest challenge at ADIPEC 2026, where Abu Dhabi unveiled ambitious AI partnerships with ADNOC and G42.
articles.body: ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — At the opening of the world's largest energy conference in Abu Dhabi, artificial intelligence took center stage alongside oil and gas as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman joined senior UAE officials for the announcement of a major partnership aimed at bringing advanced AI into the energy industry. The opening ceremony of ADIPEC 2026, attended by Fox News Digital, brought together senior government officials and energy industry leaders at a time when the war involving Iran and disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz have placed extraordinary pressure on global energy supplies. But amid discussions about oil production, shipping routes and energy security, Dr. Sultan Al Jaber, the UAE’s minister of industry and advanced technology and chief executive of state-owned energy giant ADNOC, delivered a different challenge to the technology industry. OIL SQUEEZE TIGHTENS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS CRIPPLE HORMUZ ESCAPE ROUTES "From the moment ChatGPT was born, the world has asked what energy can do for AI. And now, together, we will find out what AI can do for energy," Al Jaber told the audience, introducing a partnership between ADNOC, OpenAI and Abu Dhabi-based technology company G42. The announcement marked a significant step in the UAE’s ambition to become a global center for artificial intelligence, using its energy resources, financial strength and growing partnerships with American technology companies to help shape the industry’s future. Yet the question of what AI can actually deliver for the energy industry goes beyond the technology announcements. THE AI REVOLUTION WILL GO WHEREVER THERE'S ELECTRICITY — AND CHINA KNOWS IT Speaking exclusively to Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the conference, Dr. Angela Wilkinson, secretary general and CEO of the World Energy Council, said the most encouraging element of the presentations by Altman and Al Jaber was their focus on the role of people. "That it isn’t about AI taking decisions for humanity, it’s about AI enabling people to make better decisions," Wilkinson said. Wilkinson argued that the growing relationship between energy and AI should be understood not simply as a way to automate industrial processes, but as an opportunity to expand human capabilities. "I think what really cheered me up most is the recognition that it’s a people-centric conversation on both sides of the equation," she said. ONE OF AMERICA'S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS SAYS AI IS CREATING JOBS — NOT REPLACING THEM Amos Hochstein, a managing partner at TWG Global and a former senior adviser to President Joe Biden, welcomed the potential benefits of the new OpenAI-UAE partnership but warned that the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence must be balanced against its financial and societal costs. Speaking to Fox News Digital at ADIPEC, Hochstein said, "The energy sector is going to be one of the big beneficiaries of AI coming into the sector." But he cautioned that the U.S. must remain a leader in advanced AI while ensuring Americans are not left paying the price for its expansion, calling on the Trump administration to work more closely with industry and other sectors of society to maximize the benefits and minimize the risks. The ADNOC partnership is intended to connect advanced AI systems across the company’s operations, from oilfield development and reservoir management to refining, logistics and commercial trading. According to ADNOC, one of the initial applications will bring together decades of information from thousands of oil wells, multiple reservoirs and hundreds of facilities, with the goal of completing complex development plans in hours rather than months. The company says the technology could improve operational efficiency, lower costs and help energy producers respond more quickly to changing market conditions. Those projected improvements have not yet been independently demonstrated. For the UAE, the initiative represents something larger than a single agreement. AI ISN’T JUST A PROBLEM, IT’S A SOLUTION. SOME PEOPLE ARE ALREADY MAKING THE MOST OF IT The country is already a partner in the planned Stargate UAE project, a major computing infrastructure initiative involving American technology companies. The project is part of Abu Dhabi’s broader effort to establish itself as an international AI hub. In a separate interview with Fox News Digital in Dubai, Mohammed Baharoon, director general of the research center B’huth, described the country’s technological ambitions as an evolution from exporting barrels of oil to exporting digital computing capacity. Baharoon said the rise of AI could produce an economic transformation comparable to previous industrial revolutions, creating new industries and opportunities even as existing professions are disrupted. But he cautioned that governments are struggling to keep pace with the technology’s development. "We will need to bring in the concepts of regulation at the point of development, not after the development has happened," Baharoon told Fox News Digital. He argued that governments and technology companies need to begin addressing potential dangers while systems are being created, rather than waiting until they have already entered widespread use. THE BIGGEST THREAT IN AMERICA'S RACE WITH CHINA ISN'T BEIJING, TECH EXECUTIVE WARNS The question of human control was also central to Altman’s remarks at ADIPEC. During a panel, Altman argued that AI should remain a tool serving people rather than replacing human decision-making. The OpenAI chief also acknowledged a fundamental challenge facing his own industry: the enormous amount of energy required to power increasingly capable AI systems. Asked to identify his biggest challenge, Altman answered with a single word: "Energy." The exchange illustrated the complicated relationship between two industries that are becoming increasingly dependent on each other. AI companies need vast quantities of electricity to operate data centers, while energy producers are increasingly looking to AI to improve efficiency, optimize production and identify vulnerabilities before they disrupt supplies. AI BOOM: DEMAND FOR DATA CENTERS DRIVES INNOVATION BY ENERGY, TECH INDUSTRIES TO PRODUCE NEW POWER SOURCES The stakes are particularly high in the Gulf, where the war involving Iran and disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have forced energy producers to reconsider how they protect infrastructure and ensure supplies reach international markets. In his opening address, Al Jaber warned that nearly a billion barrels had been drawn from global oil inventories since the disruption of Hormuz, illustrating how quickly geopolitical instability can affect global energy supplies. The ADNOC chief presented artificial intelligence as one element of a broader effort to strengthen operational resilience, arguing that companies must develop systems capable of anticipating problems rather than simply responding after disruptions occur. ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM Altman, meanwhile, praised the UAE’s commitment to adopting AI across government and industry, describing it as the world’s most forward-looking country in embracing the technology. For Abu Dhabi, the emerging partnership between its traditional energy industry and the world’s leading AI companies offers an opportunity to extend its economic influence beyond oil exports. But whether these investments ultimately deliver the promised improvements in productivity, energy security and technological innovation remains to be seen. articles.title: In 2009, Ashton Kutcher co-founded a nonprofit to protect children online; by mid-2026, its technology had flagged nearly 1.4 million suspected abuse files in six months and was used by agencies in 40 countries
articles.summary: Technology has made it easier for children to connect with the world, but it has also created new ways for predators to exploit them.
articles.body: Technology has made it easier for children to connect with the world, but it has also created new ways for predators to exploit them. Tackling this problem requires more than removing harmful content after it appears online. It also involves identifying victims, helping investigators trace abuse and giving technology companies tools to detect exploitation. This challenge prompted actor Ashton Kutcher and Demi Moore to establish the DNA Foundation in 2009, which later became Thorn: Digital Defenders of Children, a technology-driven nonprofit focused on protecting children from sexual exploitation online.According to Thorn's August 11, 2026, mid-year impact update and its retrospective, Thorn at Ten: A Decade of Progress, the organisation detected 1,399,479 suspected child sexual abuse material (CSAM) files between January and June 2026. Its victim identification tools were also being used by 1,046 law enforcement agencies during the same period. Separately, Thorn's 2025 impact figures reported that its victim identification technology was being used in 40 countries. These figures highlight how the organisation has expanded its work from an initial anti-trafficking initiative into a wider effort to use technology against online child sexual abuse.From the DNA Foundation to ThornKutcher and Moore established the DNA Foundation in 2009 after learning about the scale of child sex trafficking and exploitation. Their initial focus was on raising awareness and bringing together organisations that could help prevent trafficking and protect vulnerable children.In November 2012, the foundation adopted the name Thorn: Digital Defenders of Children and refined its mission to focus more closely on the role of technology in child sexual exploitation. The organisation recognised that digital platforms could be used by offenders to target children, distribute abusive material and extend exploitation across geographical boundaries.Thorn subsequently began working with technology companies, researchers, law enforcement agencies and other child protection organisations to develop tools that could help identify victims and detect abusive content. One of its early initiatives was the Thorn Technology Task Force, which brought technology companies together to explore solutions to online child exploitation.How its technology helps investigatorsA major part of Thorn's work involves helping law enforcement identify children depicted in suspected abuse material. Its Spotlight tool was developed to assist investigators in finding victims of child sex trafficking and exploitation. By organising information and helping investigators examine evidence more efficiently, the technology can reduce the time spent identifying children who may still be experiencing abuse.The organisation also develops tools for technology companies to detect child sexual abuse material on their platforms. Its Safer product helps content-hosting services detect, review and report suspected abusive material. These tools are intended to prevent such content from spreading and reduce the repeated victimisation of children whose abuse has been documented and circulated online.Thorn's 2026 mid-year update reported that its technology processed more than 1.09 trillion files between January and June to detect suspected child sexual abuse material. During this period, it identified nearly 1.4 million suspected CSAM files and 470,521 suspected instances of child sexual exploitation. The organisation also reported that 86 companies were using its CSAM detection products. These figures represent suspected material and instances identified by its systems, rather than a confirmed count of individual victims or proven criminal cases.Expanding research and child safety effortsThorn's work extends beyond detection technology. It also conducts research into how children experience the internet and how online exploitation methods are changing. Its 2025 Youth Perspectives Report examined young people's online experiences, including emerging patterns involving artificial intelligence and access to age-restricted platforms.In the first half of 2026, the organisation also published research on Sadistic Online Exploitation, examining how violent online networks exploit weaknesses in existing child protection systems. The findings are intended to help investigators, technology companies, policymakers and caregivers better understand emerging risks. Another development during this period was the integration of Thorn's Grooming Detection technology into Hive's moderation platform. The organisation also introduced Context Labels to its Safer product, giving safety professionals additional information to assess suspected abusive content and prioritise investigations.Thorn's international reach has grown alongside these initiatives. Its 2025 impact report recorded that victim identification tools were being used in 40 countries, while its mid-2026 update reported 1,046 law enforcement agencies using its child victim detection tools.The organisation's progress reflects a broader shift in child protection, where technology companies, investigators and researchers increasingly need to work together. Although detecting suspected abusive material is only one part of the response, Thorn's work aims to help identify victims sooner, limit the circulation of harmful content and strengthen safeguards for children navigating the digital world.You use AI every day. articles.title: Dutch small boat launch shows smugglers adapting, says Dover MP
articles.summary: Dover MP Mike Tapp says smugglers will find new launch locations and methods due to disruptions.
articles.body:
Dover MP Mike Tapp says smugglers will keep adapting after it was discovered that a boat stopped in the Channel with 38 migrants on board had launched from the Netherlands.

Prosecutors have confirmed the vessel that was found floating with no engine near Cadzand on Saturday had entered the water from Dutch territory.

This year crossings have already been attempted along a wider stretch of coast from Belgium to Normandy.

The UK government said that overall crossings were down significantly this year.

"As launch disruptions grow, the criminal gangs will adapt and a part of that will be finding new launch locations and methods," said Tapp.

"That means our operational efforts must also be agile.

"We have seen a significant reduction in crossings this year, but we still have a long way to go."

Bastiaan van Blokland, from the Netherlands Red Cross, said the crossing was "unusual" and "didn't look safe at all", adding "we don't see these things often, if at all".

"The situation definitely was dire, 38 people on a boat with legs dangling out of the boat, in the cold weather, without an engine," he said.

"We were surprised that this situation occurred, we are not very familiar with these kind of movements and we will be alert for the future."

Two men are still being questioned on suspicion of people smuggling, police said.

Small boat smuggling attempts have increased from 2018 and beaches around areas of Calais and Dunkirk in Northern France have tended to be the traditional launch points.

Federal Belgian police suggested it had been due to French enforcement activity.

Police officials in the Netherlands described the small boat rescue as rare.

However, there have been a small number of cases in recent years where smugglers have been caught trying to use yachts to smuggle migrants into the UK from the Dutch coast.

The UK government said this year had seen the lowest number of summer arrivals - a period when journeys often rise in part due to the warmer weather - since 2020.

Last week crossings resumed after three weeks of stormy weather.

Former director general of the UK Border Force Tony Smith said it was "clear that the human smugglers operating in Europe continue to try new routes to bring illegal entrants to the UK".

"In recent months we have seen launches from the Normandy beaches, Belgium and now as far afield as the Netherlands rather than across the short straits to Dover under the original model," he said.

"It is important that the Border Security Command adapt its operations to cope with this ever expanding challenge."

The government said in October that the home secretary had signed a deal with the Belgian interior minister enabling police in both countries to exchange intelligence more quickly to disrupt and dismantle organised criminal networks, including those involved in migrant smuggling.

Nearly 1,050 French officers are now supporting UK-France efforts to stop crossings, with an additional new surge team bolstering operations on Western beaches, according to officials.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "Joint efforts with international partners have prevented over 50,000 crossing attempts and seized 1,100 boats and engines since the election.

"But we must go further. That's why we are boosting the number of officers on the ground in France and removing the pull factors drawing people here through illegal and dangerous routes."

articles.title: Blood sugar spikes could hinge on the order you eat your food, study suggests
articles.summary: Meal sequencing with olive oil may help blunt blood sugar spikes, a mouse study suggests, but a registered dietitian says it's not a quick fix for humans.
articles.body: A simple change to the order in which you eat could help blunt blood sugar spikes, new research suggests, but experts say it's not necessarily a "quick fix." In a study published in the journal Diabetes in October, mice that received olive oil 15 minutes before glucose — a simple sugar the body uses for energy — had a smaller early rise in blood sugar than mice given glucose first or glucose alone. The researchers also saw the effect in mice with type 2 diabetes and severe insulin deficiency. The researchers also tested other dietary fats, suggesting the response may not be unique to olive oil. The experiment offers clues about why food order may matter. BUTTER, BEEF TALLOW DEBATE ISN'T OVER AS HEART EXPERTS WARN OF RISKS AND US GUIDELINES DIFFER ON FATS "Our findings suggest that the order in which nutrients reach the gut can engage a coordinated hormone-nerve response that changes how quickly the stomach delivers glucose to the intestine," corresponding author Dr. Daisuke Yabe of Kyoto University said in a statement. When the mice received fat before sugar, their stomachs released food into the intestine more slowly and their blood sugar rose less sharply at first. THE 8 HEALTHIEST BEANS YOU SHOULD BE EATING MORE OFTEN, ACCORDING TO NUTRITION EXPERT The researchers also found that giving the mice fat first triggered early increases in two hormones, glucagon and GLP-1. Although glucagon is usually known for raising blood sugar, the researchers found that the two hormones appear to work together to help limit the rise in glucose. Yabe said the group's research is inspired by practical approaches people can sustain. "Meal-sequencing is appealing because it merely changes how a meal is eaten rather than requiring people to avoid entire food groups," he said. BEST FOODS FOR REDUCING DANGEROUS BELLY FAT AND PROTECTING HEART HEALTH The researchers, however, said further studies are needed to test meal sequencing in people. The study adds to research on how food order may offer a practical way to moderate blood sugar, Huma Chaudhry, a Chicago-based registered dietitian and founder of Dose of Nutrition, told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Chaudhry also cautioned, however, that since the study was conducted on mice, "We can't assume the same results would occur in humans." Previous human research suggests eating vegetables or protein before carbohydrates may also help moderate post-meal blood sugar, while more research is needed on olive oil specifically, she said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "The takeaway isn't that everyone should start drinking olive oil before a meal," she said, adding that there is "no need to treat it like a supplement or quick fix." "The bigger message is about building balanced meals that naturally contain healthy fats, protein, fiber and carbohydrates," Chaudhry added. The mice were fasted overnight and received olive oil and glucose separately, 15 minutes apart, which is different from people eating a typical balanced meal. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Chaudhry suggested starting with a leafy green salad dressed with olive oil before pasta, or pairing eggs with toast at breakfast. Food sequencing doesn't require separating foods by a set interval, Chaudhry said. At dinner, for instance, someone might eat a salad dressed in olive oil first and then have chicken and pasta, which can raise blood sugar, together. "Food order may influence blood sugar alongside the overall quality and balance of our meals," she said. Aberdeen DJ and hip-hop producer Vagrant Real Estate has won the 2026 Scottish Album of the Year award.

A moniker for Nick Cronin, Vagrant Real Estate triumphed with "Neither Collar Nor Crown".

He scooped the £20,000 first prize after emerging from a shortlist which included Barry Can't Swim and Hen Hoose Collective.

"This is a bit mad, I fully did not expect this at all," he said.

Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds

Recent winners of the award have included Kai Reesu last year, Redolent in 2024, and Young Fathers the year before - which was their third win.

The Scottish Album of the Year (SAY) Award was held in Dundee's Caird Hall on Thursday night.

"Neither Collar Nor Crown" brought together 25 Scottish artists from different genres.

Vagrant Real Estate has been independently releasing music since 2018.

He samples traditional Scottish folk and Gaelic, merged with Scottish rap and hip-hop.

Vagrant Real Estate thanked the judging panel on stage, and said: "The shortlist was unbelievable this year - there's so much talent in this country.

"The album is full of collaborators from all across the country.

"I just want to say to anybody who's trying to make a career in music who doesn't live on the central belt where you might feel the industry's attention is - I'm from Aberdeen. Let's go."

Robert Kilpatrick, creative director of the Scottish Music Industry Association (SMIA), said: "Bringing together 25 Scottish artists, it's an unapologetically Scottish record that pushes the boundaries of Scottish hip-hop while drawing deeply from our shared cultural and musical heritage."

Nikhita was named The Sound of Young Scotland, winning a funding package worth up to £10,000.

And Boards of Canada - originally from Cullen in Moray - won the Modern Scottish Classic Award for their 1998 debut album "Music Has The Right to Children".

articles.title: Doomscrolling (and kids) destroyed my reading habit. Could the ‘Booker Challenge’ save it?
articles.summary: With two young kids, two phones and a roughly-two-minute attention span, I tried to read the entire Booker Prize shortlist in seven weeks.
articles.body: Novels are an endangered art form. In the early 1990s, more than 60% of American adults finished at least one book a year; today, fewer than half do. Gen Z often takes the heat for this decline, but we’re all to blame — including me, a time-poor millennial with two young kids, two phones and a roughly-two-minute attention span. Each January, for the last few years, I have set myself a (what I thought to be) perfectly achievable New Year’s resolution: to read, for the sake of pleasure alone, 12 books in 12 months. And each fall, for the last few years, I found myself behind schedule and shamelessly attempting to game my own challenge. What if I blasted through some poetry to make up the numbers? And plays counts, right? They’re technically books but are short enough, almost by definition, to finish in one sitting. Just like that, the joy of reading I’d hoped to rekindle was lost. Instead of offering an escape, literature had become a source of angst. In our over-optimized age, where “microlearning” apps promise to condense books into bullet points that can be injected, via AirPods, into our saturated minds, picking up a novel felt like a lapse of productivity — or a guilty pleasure to contemplate before spending an hour mindlessly doomscrolling. As a journalist, I consume plenty of non-fiction (though I often skim-read for efficiency’s sake). I also read a staggering number of children’s books. In my own time, however, I still feel an unrelenting pressure for books to serve professional interests or make me — or, at least, make me feel — smarter. What I needed was a strict deadline, an expectant editor and an excuse to read make-believe professionally. Enter my entirely self-directed “Booker Challenge.” On September 22, the Booker Prize unveiled its annual shortlist. These are, in theory, the year’s six best novels. Although originally for British, Irish and Commonwealth writers, the prize is now open to all English-language books and considered the most prestigious accolade for a single work of fiction. For this year’s longlist, the jury got through over 160 books in six months. One judge, historian Mary Beard, has said that this meant working “harder than I have ever done before.” But surely reading the six-book shortlist, in the seven weeks before the winner’s announcement, wouldn’t be that difficult? Their combined 2,000-plus pages, I calculated, amounted to a very manageable 45 pages a day. Reading app Swiftread told me this would take the average reader just 1.3 hours. My iPhone’s nagging Screen Time notifications, meanwhile, told me that I spend longer — much longer — than that staring at my devices each day. It may feel like I have no free time, but it turns out I, objectively, do. I could complete my challenge and still have a few hours left to doomscroll. Escapism of yore My anxiety around reading has snowballed since becoming a dad in 2024. But while my kids are obviously significant (and welcome!) consumers of my diminished downtime, I cannot blame parenthood for my failures. In truth, my once-healthy reading habit has been under assault since 2011. The inaugural culprit: my very first iPhone. As a teen in the pre-smartphone era, I would devour fiction, both classic and contemporary, wherever I could. Traveling to school by train — and with no way to check my Myspace for the latest updates — I would frequently lose myself in fictional worlds, there and back. Now, my commute involves the routine carousel of Instagram, Reddit, news, Slack, soccer results, already-read WhatsApp messages and then back to Instagram again. In the past 15 years, I have normalized mild repetitive strain injuries to my right thumb, and that shameful feeling of mechanically reopening an app that I’d only just closed because my brain has short-circuited the order in which I’m supposed to deliver it dopamine microdoses. I have normalized the déjà vu of scrolling past the same content twice because I didn’t give the algorithm enough time to refresh. This year’s Booker Prize shortlist offered a tantalizing return to the escapism of yore. Its six books promised to take me from a medieval royal court to a post-alien-invasion-near-future, via 1980s Jamaica, 1990s Scotland, 2020s Massachusetts and present-day London. For the first time in a long time, I felt excited to read. I began with the prize’s two favorites, both written by former winners. Leading the pack, Marlon James’ “The Disappearers” charts the devastating fallout of a homophobic attack on a theater rehearsal in Kingston, Jamaica that leaves one dead, one maimed and, soon after, two missing. Masterfully told through letters, journals, interview transcripts and monologues, the monumental 600-page story placed me deep in the psyches of men grappling with the unceasing threat of violence. The bookmaker’s second-favorite, Douglas Stuart’s “John of John,” is similarly engrossing — albeit in an entirely different way. This time, I was transported to the remote Scottish island of Harris, where an arts graduate returns home to his strict, pious father and the repressive (and repressed) Presbyterian nest he thought he had flown. It is quietly gripping and beautifully written. Both books would be worthy winners. They are also the two longest. But, invigorated by my challenge, I felt a warm nostalgia carrying the heavy tomes under my arm everywhere I went. Hoping to forge new routines, I snuck in chapters at my son’s swimming class, the doctor’s waiting room, and the office during lunch. I smugly enjoyed being the only person on the bus not staring at a screen. At home, where my infant daughter decided she would only nap in my arms, I found that a large paperback book fit perfectly on top of her tiny torso. When she was asleep in her crib, I read under my bedcovers with a nightlight. Old habits die hard For the first three weeks, I hit my 45-page average with ease. Overperforming on weekends helped offset busier midweeks. Then, my first major obstacle: a 0-page day. Forgive me: It was my birthday and I was hungover. I didn’t want to read. My mind immediately began its familiar mental gymnastics. Do I need 90 pages tomorrow to catch up? Or do I just read a couple extra a day, from now on, to compensate? Is this suddenly becoming less fun? Upping my daily target to 47 pages, the challenge continued apace. On vacation, I read American author Elizabeth Strout’s “The Things We Never Say,” the tender tale of an affable middle-aged schoolteacher with suicidal thoughts, an urge to shoplift and a burdensome family secret. I then power through M. John Harrison’s wonderfully inscrutable “The End of Everything,” which imagines a partially collapsed society following an invasion by mysterious beings whose activities and intentions are beyond human understanding (AI, anyone?). Next up is debut novelist Rebecca Perry’s impressive “May We Feed the King,” a dual narrative that flits between a museum curator and a medieval monarch — reluctantly and unexpectedly thrust onto the throne following the death of his older brothers — whom she is researching. I enjoyed them all, for unique and varied reasons. And yet, old habits die hard. Sometimes, I found myself hiding my phone inside my book, so my wife didn’t realize when I had erred. Some days, I looked forward to after-dinner reading, but others I just wanted an early night or to vegetate by way of streaming. As the challenge trundled on, the harder it became. I began experiencing a sense of relief when a chapter’s final page was revealed to be mostly white space, or when a new section started afresh on the next spread. This was no reflection of the books’ quality. In fact, the final nominee I read, “Black Bag” by Luke Kennard, was among my favorites — a gloriously surreal but relatable story of an out-of-work actor hired to attend college while zipped in a leather bag for a psychological experiment. The problem was becoming clear: In our over-optimized age, I had just created another metric to agonize over. ‘Attention rehabilitation’ The reading slowdown is a global phenomenon. In Singapore, where I am writing this from, a government campaign against “brainrot” is paying people to read for 15 minutes a day. As a non-citizen, I am ineligible for the cash (which only amounts to about 80 US cents for 50 consecutive days), but I joined a series of accompanying talks hosted by the country’s National Library Board. In one, Richard Cytowic, a neurologist who only checks his email twice a day, warned that humans can’t really multitask — we just rapidly move between tasks, with each switch costing us time, attention and energy. Interruptions leave us with what he called “attention residue,” because returning to complicated matters means having to reconstruct the mental context we built before the interruption. “Deep reading,” he said, “asks the brain to do what endless scrolling prevents: Remain with one thing long enough for meaning to accumulate.” Reading also puts the “tempo of attention” back in our hands, argued Cytowic, who authored the book “Your Stone Age Brain in the Screen Age.” “We may pause, reread, wonder or allow an image to develop — nothing advances automatically,” he said, adding: “Reading is far more than an escape from distraction. It is rehabilitation for an attention system that has presently been trained to expect one interruption after another.” He is less enthusiastic, however, about target-based approaches. Has my Booker Challenge, to use his words, turned “rest into another performance, a step count, a meditation streak, a podcast consumed at the double speed”? Should I, in his words again, learn to “tolerate a few minutes that cannot be measured, optimized or displayed as an achievement”? Probably. I have been a journalist long enough to know that I respond best to deadlines. I feel I have achieved plenty of “deep reading,” and I am struck with genuine satisfaction whenever I see the completed tomes stacked on my bedside table. But this challenge has come at a cost. Other parts of my life have, indubitably, suffered. Over the last seven weeks, I have slept far less than is recommended by medical professionals. I am woefully underprepared for the half-marathon I signed up for. My midweek social life has shriveled, from negligible to non-existent. A growing pile of untouched magazines and weekend newspapers (yes, actual paper ones) stands testament to everything I didn’t read. And while I was confident that I hadn’t neglected my parental duties, I noted my wife’s subtly barbed response when — using my Booker challenge as evidence — I reassured a friend over dinner that the arrival of his second child didn’t have to spell the end of his free time. “I’m happy for you,” she said from the other end of the table, not quite rolling her eyes. Like most things in life, the key to being a better reader is likely small, regular doses, rather than sudden intense bursts pegged to major news events. Perhaps, next time, I will give myself the whole year to read the shortlist. Perhaps I’ll join a book club or BookTok, or enlist friends to join me on the journey. Or perhaps I’ll just follow Singapore’s 15-minutes-a-day approach, even if I can’t collect my 80 cents.

articles.title: Kenyan cult leader sentenced to 200 years in prison over the deaths of 190 children
articles.summary: A Kenyan cult leader has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murder of 191 people, all but one of them children, in a campaign of abuse and forced fasting.
articles.body: A Kenyan cult leader has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murder of 191 people, all but one of them children, in a campaign of abuse and forced fasting. Paul Mackenzie, founder of the Good News International Church, was sentenced Friday alongside more than two dozen others at the Mombasa High Court. Mackenzie preached that the world would end in August 2023 and that followers needed to fast in order to reach heaven. According to a Kenyan Senate report into the deaths, his teachings were based on “doomsday or end-times” beliefs. Children were scheduled to die first, followed by young people and women. Men were expected to stay alive long enough to bury the bodies before dying. Mackenzie’s sentencing comprised of 100 years’ imprisonment for the murder of those who starved and 100 years for those who died by direct homicide. In her sentencing remarks, Lady Justice Diana Kavedza said she did not impose the death penalty because it could strengthen the convicts’ belief that dying would reunite them with Jesus, rather than deter them. She also wanted to leave open the possibility that they could help locate the remains of missing children. “In the respectful view of this court, such a sentence (the death penalty) would therefore fail to achieve deterrence,” she said. Kavedza said 161 of the victims were children aged 9 or younger. Twenty-two were between 10 and 13 years old, and five were between 14 and 16. The ages of two others could not be established. She also said that several of the convicts’ children remained missing and were presumed dead. The judge added that 183 of the 191 victims died from starvation, including 182 children and one adult. The remaining eight victims, all children, were suffocated, strangled or beaten to death. Mackenzie had persuaded followers to abandon their homes and move to Shakahola Forest, in eastern Kenya, promising that fasting there would bring them closer to God and prepare them for heaven. The court found that religious teachings were used to enforce the fast. Guards controlled followers’ movements and prevented them from leaving. Those who resisted were forced to comply, while children were restrained, denied food and punished when they tried to eat or escape. Mackenzie was convicted of murder last month. In her ruling, Kavedza described how he used sermons and written materials to convince followers that the outside world was evil and that salvation could only be found in the forest. Messages extracted from his phone, including WhatsApp exchanges, showed that he had communicated with followers before they’d moved to Shakahola Forest. Kavedza said most of those convicted hadn’t shown any remorse for their actions. Mackenzie smiled several times during Friday’s sentencing. Survivors testified that deaths in the forest were celebrated as “weddings to Jesus,” with those who died regarded as “heroes of faith,” Kavedza said. Postmortem findings cited by the judge showed that starvation was not the only cause of death. Some victims died from suffocation, neck compression or head injuries. Authorities began exhuming bodies from Shakahola in April 2023 after reports that people had died while following Mackenzie’s teachings. They have recovered more than 400 bodies so far. The 191 murder convictions relate to the victims in the case decided last month, while further charges could follow. Stephen Mwiti, whose six children died in Shakahola, told Reuters that his wife had taken his family there to fast. She was among those convicted in the case. Questioning the decision to make children fast, Mwiti said: “Even if the adults had agreed to fast, what about the children?” He said no outcome in the case could undo the loss of his family. Rodgers Shibutse, a Nairobi resident who identified his mother’s remains among those exhumed in February 2024, told CNN after the sentencing Friday: “I cannot say that I am 100% satisfied. It (the verdict) is not enough to pay for the life of my mum, but we have no other choice. At least, he (Mackenzie) cannot finish the 200 years in jail and will die eventually.” This story has been updated with developments.

articles.title: Dog fight trainer banned from owning animals for 15 years
articles.summary: Sean Alexander Mullen's Patterdale terrier was found with serious facial injuries by the Scottish SPCA.
articles.body:
A man has been given a 15-year ban on owning animals after training a dog for animal fighting.

Sean Alexander Mullen's Patterdale terrier, called Ronnie, was found with serious facial injuries by the Scottish SPCA.

Mullen, who had 11 previous convictions including one for bludgeoning a fox to death, was given the ban on caring for, and owning, animals and was ordered to carry out 200 hours of unpaid work.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

The SSPCA's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) carried out a search at Mullen's Paisley home after being tipped off about Ronnie's condition.

They found the dog and two younger male Patterdale terriers, along with animal fighting paraphernalia and training equipment, such as treadmills.

Ronnie was found with severe facial injuries consistent with having been in face-to-face combat with wild animals.

A vet who examined the animals said Ronnie had "repeated facial trauma" that most likely came from animal fighting.

The vet added: "Allowing the dog to sustain these injuries resulted in preventable disease and injury.

"The wounds would have been painful and required veterinary treatment. By not seeking veterinary attention, the dog was left to endure severe unnecessary suffering for weeks, or for however long the injuries had been present."

An SIU inspector said the charity welcomed the sentencing but was disappointed a lifetime ban and a custodial sentence were not imposed.

The unit called on the Scottish government to introduce animal welfare sentencing guidelines, similar to those in England.

Ronnie's new owner described the terrier as being a "bundle of love".

They added: "He is the cutest and loveliest dog. He is so caring and loving. He has brought utter joy to our lives.

"I really can't understand why anyone would do something like this. It brings me to tears to think of the pain and suffering Ronnie has gone through".

Mullen was also sentenced to a restriction of liberty order from 19:00 to 07:00 for six months, reduced from nine months.

articles.title: Tanzania court jails opposition leader for incitement, lifts treason charge
articles.summary: Dismissal of treason charge means Tundu Lissu avoids threat of death penalty.
articles.body:
A Tanzanian court has jailed opposition leader Tundu Lissu for four years on a charge of incitement.

But the three-judge panel in Dar-es-Salaam dismissed a charge of treason that carried the threat of a death sentence. The ruling was handed down on Friday, in a trial closely watched internationally.

“We are satisfied that through his statements, the accused intended to disrupt elections and instigate violence,” one judge told a courtroom packed with Lissu’s supporters.

“We sentence you to four years in prison, but the doors are open for appeal,” the judge added.

Lissu, who heads the main opposition party, Chadema, responded that the trial was “political persecution”, accusing the judges of following orders from the government of President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

“Excuses were created to imprison me,” he told the court.

“I was not charged with incitement but you judges are convicting me with it just to impress the person who gives you the titles. I believe these were directives,” he said.

Tito Magoti, a Tanzanian human rights lawyer based in Oxford, UK, said the fact that the treason charge – which is the capital crime in Tanzania’s penal code – was dismissed for Lissu is “a major blow” for the state. “It shows that there wasn’t any intention to charge him with treason, but rather to put him behind bars,” he told Al Jazeera.

Lissu was arrested before the October 2025 presidential vote, as the government carried out a wave of detentions and abductions targeting opponents and critics.

The clampdown sparked huge protests during the election, which President Hassan was declared to have won with 98 percent of the vote.

Security forces responded by killing thousands of demonstrators , according to the opposition and rights groups. The government put the death toll at 518.

“A lot of people in Tanzania will tell you that they are afraid to speak out, especially in the last two years,” said Al Jazeera’s Catherine Soi, reporting from Nairobi in neighbouring Kenya on Friday.

“Leading up to that election they said that if someone like Tundu Lissu can be convicted and put to to jail, what will happen to ordinary citizens?”

Soi said that in the past two years in Tanzania, “we have seen critics put to jail, others silenced, others have left the country, media freedoms have been curtailed, and just last week a figure from Lissu’s party was arrested and charged for treason – so there’s a lot of fear”.

“Off camera people said that many of the charges are politically motivated,” she added.

Security was heightened across Dar-es-Salaam – Tanzania’s commercial capital – and around the court before Friday’s verdict, as Lissu’s supporters gathered for the hearing.

This was the first time that Lissu, 58, faced such serious charges, despite repeated arrests.

In 2017, he survived an assassination attempt in which he was shot 16 times, an attack he believes was politically motivated and which required him to undergo nearly 20 surgeries.

The treason case drew criticism from British and European Union lawmakers, who described it as politically motivated and called for Lissu’s immediate release.

It marked the third high-profile treason trial in mainland Tanzania’s history.

The first two, in the 1970s and 1980s, involved defendants accused of plotting to overthrow and assassinate the country’s founding president, Julius Nyerere.

articles.title: More than 40 pilot whales die in ‘distressing’ mass stranding on New Zealand coast
articles.summary: More than 40 pilot whales have died on a New Zealand coast following a mass stranding that rescuers have described as “difficult and distressing.”
articles.body: More than 40 pilot whales have died on a New Zealand beach following a mass stranding that rescuers described as “difficult and distressing.” The pod of pilot whales was found stranded on the Ngawi coast near the village of Cape Palliser on the southern tip of New Zealand’s North Island just after 8 a.m. local time on Thursday, the country’s Department of Conservation (DOC) said in a statement posted on Facebook that morning. At the time, at least 20 whales were known to be ashore, with four still alive, the environmental organization Project Jonah New Zealand said in a post on Facebook that afternoon. The charity added that it was working with the DOC and the local iwi, a group of Māori tribes, to conduct health assessments and prepare for the living whales to be refloated at high tide. However, in an update on Friday afternoon local time, the DOC said a total of 43 whales were found on the Ngawi to Mangatoetoe coast and “unfortunately none of these are believed to have survived.” Many of the whales, covering “several kilometres of coastline,” were already dead when they were discovered, and those found alive “succumbed throughout the day,” Project Jonah said in its own update. “It was a difficult and distressing event for those who were involved in the response,” the charity said. “We are grateful to the locals who were first on the scene and supported the whales that were found alive, keeping them cool and as comfortable as possible.” The DOC said it is “now working with iwi to manage the burial of the taonga,” or highly prized heritage. North Island’s southern coastline is “exposed to the powerful swells of Cook Strait,” Project Jonah said. These conditions, combined with the loose gravel beaches and “sharp” rocks, made the environment “especially challenging,” and the remoteness of the location further challenged responders. ‘Very sad’ and ‘strange’ Fisherman Andrew Sim described the incident as “very sad.” He told CNN affiliate RNZ Thursday that he had spent more than four decades on the coast and had witnessed whale strandings before but had never seen pilot whales come ashore. “It’s most strange that they’ve come in here, there’s just no reason for it, to be honest. Just bad luck, I don’t know,” Sim said. Pilot whales are “prolific stranders,” according to the DOC, but what causes mass strandings is not well understood. “They happen to species which tend to be highly social and it is likely that all or part of a social group becomes stranded at the same time,” Ian L. Boyd, professor of biology at the University of St. Andrews, Scotland, and former chief scientific adviser at the UK’s Department of Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, said in a statement shared with CNN Friday by the Science Media Centre. “Mass strandings can tend to happen in particular locations often where there is a shallow shelving coastline,” Boyd added. “It is possible that a whole social group gets disorientated and caught by a falling tide, but this is almost certainly only part of much more complex set of causes.” Pilot whales’ highly social behavior means that if one whale loses its way then others come to its aid, according to the DOC, which said the “most likely” theory for mass strandings is that the animals’ echolocation is not well-suited to shallow, sloping waters. It is currently summer in New Zealand, which is when the whales follow common food sources inshore and when most mass strandings occur. The largest pilot whale stranding in the country involved an estimated 1,000 whales at the Chatham Islands in 1918, according to the DOC. Several mass stranding events in Oceania have garnered attention in the last few years. In 2022, around 500 pilot whales died in mass strandings near shark-infested waters on remote New Zealand islands. In February last year, more than 150 whales beached off the coast of Tasmania, Australia – and all of them either died or were euthanized – in the first mass stranding of the animals in Tasmania in 50 years. The previous year, 28 pilot whales died after around 160 whales beached off the coast of Western Australia. The majority of the pod were returned to sea.

articles.title: Austrian police investigate man for leaving 17-year-old on Germany's highest mountain Zugspitze
articles.summary: The teenager was eventually rescued on Zugspitze and has since been discharged from hospital.
articles.body:
Austrian police are investigating a German man aged 21 on suspicion of endangering public safety, after his 17-year-old female friend was left stranded on Germany's highest mountain Zugspitze in sub-zero temperatures.

The teenager called emergency services and was eventually rescued on the mountain at an altitude of about 2,500m (8,200ft).

She was suffering from hypothermia and taken to hospital in nearby Garmisch-Partenkirchen, over the border in Germany, before being discharged.

In Austria, anyone who endangers another person's physical safety can be punished with up to three months in prison.

The pair set off in the early hours of Sunday from the resort of Ehrwald in the Austrian Tyrol with the aim of seeing the sunrise on Zugspitze.

Temperatures that morning had fallen to -12C, a mountain rescuer told German Press Agency DPA.

The weather was so poor that the two climbers were soon knee-deep in snow, according to Austrian reports, and their plans to reach the 2,962m summit soon changed.

At one point they separated and the 21-year-old descended alone. The reason they split is unclear, and a police spokesperson declined to comment, citing the ongoing investigation.

Seven mountain rescuers responded to the call, and a helicopter eventually airlifted the teenager off the mountain. She was then taken to hospital by ambulance.

Although the teenager survived, what happened on Zugspitze on Sunday is reminiscent of a fatal incident on Austria's highest peak, the Grossglockner, in January 2025.

A 33-year-old woman froze to death on the Grossglockner after her boyfriend left her on the mountain, and he was later found guilty of grossly negligent manslaughter.

The boyfriend had insisted he had left her there while trying to get help, telling the court he had loved his girlfriend and that he was deeply sorry.

The case reverberated throughout the mountaineering community at the time, with prosecutors arguing that as the more experienced climber, he was the responsible guide on the trip and had failed to turn back or call for help in time.

In the latest case in Austria, police have said once they have completed their investigation, a report will be sent to Innsbruck public prosecutors, who will decide if a criminal offence has been committed.

articles.title: ‘City of immigrants’: Who is Nithya Raman, the Los Angeles mayor-elect?
articles.summary: The two biggest cities in the US will now be led by Indian-origin immigrants – both democratic socialists.
articles.body:
Nithya Raman, mayor-elect of Los Angeles, held back tears as the enormity of her victory began to sink in.

“This city has given me and my family so much,” Raman, an Indian-born urban planner who came to the United States at the age of six, told supporters in Los Angeles on Thursday night, after projections showed her winning the mayoral race .

“The idea that Angelenos voted for an immigrant to be their next mayor at this moment in American history is so deeply moving to me,” the 45-year-old said.

Raman’s victory means that three of the world’s most influential cities – New York, Los Angeles and London – will now be led by individuals of South Asian descent.

A democratic socialist, she also gives the progressive movement another leader in a major US city, after New York and Washington, DC.

The result came amid a dominant showing by Democrats in US midterm elections , in which the party wrested control of both chambers of Congress and scored its biggest landslide victory in half a century. Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which backed Raman’s campaign, also claimed an impressive series of wins , with 105 of its endorsed candidates on track to secure elected office, according to the group.

For Raman, the victory provides a bigger platform to address central planks of her political vision for the US’s second-largest city, including tackling its longstanding homelessness crisis and expanding affordable housing.

The Asian Democrats of Los Angeles County (ADLAC) congratulated Raman on becoming the first Asian-American elected to lead Los Angeles and said it looked forward to working with her to “deliver for our communities”.

“We saw a wave of change across the country this election, and Los Angeles was no exception,” ADLAC President Zahra Hajee said. “The political establishment should take note: Voters want real solutions and a government that actually works for them.”

Raman was born in the state of Keralam, in southern India, and moved to the US with her family at the age of six.

She studied at Harvard University before earning a master’s degree in urban planning from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

After completing her studies, Raman moved back to India and launched an initiative to improve urban governance in the southern city of Chennai.

In 2013, she moved to Los Angeles, where she co-founded a nonprofit organisation to support people experiencing homelessness. The organisation, SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition, stresses that unhoused people are “fellow members of our community worthy of the same dignity, respect and representation afforded to any housed person”.

Raman also spent a year as entertainment director of Time’s Up, an organisation founded by Hollywood figures to raise money for legal support for victims of sexual harassment.

Her foray into politics came in 2019, when she shocked Los Angeles’s political establishment by defeating incumbent city councilman David Ryu and becoming the first DSA-backed candidate elected to the council. She credited a major grassroots organising drive for that victory.

Raman’s run for mayor this year came as another surprise to the local political scene, as most Democratic Party leadership stuck with incumbent mayor Karen Bass. Raman entered the race at the 11th hour, reversing her earlier endorsement of one-time ally Bass. She said Los Angeles had reached a “breaking point” and was “no longer a place of opportunity for too many”.

Bass was endorsed by prominent Democrats such as California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.

Raman’s mayoral campaign focused on expanding affordable housing, addressing the city’s decades-old homelessness crisis and protecting immigrants.

Her campaign described the city’s housing crisis as “the compounding moral crisis of our time”. Growing desensitisation to homelessness, it added, “is a moral failing”.

“Every time we see one of our neighbors living and dying on the streets, we should be shocked,” a campaign policy statement said. “Instead, in Los Angeles, it has become routine.”

Raman envisions a new approach to addressing homelessness, including expanding medical teams for people living in encampments or on the streets, alongside huge new investment in housing.

She estimates her policies will halve the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments throughout the city by 2028, when the Olympic Games will come to Los Angeles. As of 2025, the city had some 44,000 homeless people, including 27,000 staying on the streets, in vehicles or encampments, according to the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority.

Raman has also pledged to replace the city’s police chief, whom she says has “lost the confidence” of residents by failing to curb federal immigration raids carried out by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency.

“Federal raids have left Angelenos afraid to live in the city they call home – where they work and raise their families,” said Raman’s campaign. “That has to stop.”

While Raman was championed by many progressive voices, she had a rift with the DSA over the organisation demanding that she not make the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel an official part of her platform.

Raman has said she believes Israel is committing “genocide” in Gaza and that the best way for Los Angeles residents to express solidarity with Palestinians is through “non-violent protest, legislative action, and diplomatic pressure, including BDS”.

In a close vote, the DSA decided against revoking the endorsement granted to Raman by its local Los Angeles chapter, and ultimately celebrated her election victory.

In her victory speech, Raman promised to restore what she called an ambitious, creative and entrepreneurial Los Angeles.

“For too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do,” she said.

Raman joins a growing number of leaders with immigrant backgrounds in global metropolises.

In New York last year, Zohran Mamdani was elected as the city’s first South Asian and Africa-born mayor. Like Raman, he has Indian roots; Mamdani’s father is a leading scholar and his mother an internationally renowned filmmaker.

Overseas, Sadiq Khan , the son of Pakistani immigrants, has been the mayor of London since 2016. And in Toronto, Olivia Chow, who moved to Canada from Hong Kong at the age of 13, has served as mayor since 2023.

Raman’s rise has drawn comparisons with Mamdani’s. Both have immigrant backgrounds, belong to the DSA and have advocated major changes to urban policy, including on housing.

Raman has said she is flattered by the comparison but is careful to distinguish herself.

“Mamdani is one of the most popular politicians in America right now, and I’m very grateful to be compared to someone who is that skilled as a communicator and a leader,” she said in an October interview with Vanity Fair.

articles.title: Kenyan court sentences starvation cult leader to 200 years
articles.summary: Paul Mackenzie and accomplices were convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult.
articles.body:
A Kenyan court has sentenced starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie to 200 years in prison for the murder of 190 children and one adult.

The sentence was comprised of 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, Justice Diana Kavedza said on Friday, as she read out the judgement. The 191 victims were starved to death on his orders and buried in a forest.

Twenty-eight accomplices, who were convicted alongside Mackenzie last month, were also sentenced to various prison terms.

The self-proclaimed pastor and ⁠⁠his Good News International Church organised a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death, so they could go to heaven before the world ended and “meet Jesus”.

His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders.

Mackenzie, wearing a grey polo shirt and black trousers, smiled as he entered a tent set up outside the court where the hearing was held.

He had denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court in Mombasa rejected his defence.

Police arrested Mackenzie in 2023 after receiving a tip-off. After several weeks, authorities began uncovering bodies in the Shakahola Forest near the coast in southeastern Kenya.

Emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

More than 400 people died in the Shakahola tragedy, according to Kenyan authorities, making it one of the country’s deadliest cult-related disasters.

The scale of the killing is comparable to that of the doomsday cult that killed more than 700 people in Uganda in 2000, and the 1978 Jonestown massacre in Guyana when an American cult leader killed more than 900 people by ordering them to drink poison.

Investigations into the Mackenzie affair uncovered mass graves and evidence of severe malnutrition, triggering nationwide scrutiny of religious violence and the government’s failure to detect the group’s activities earlier.

Since the bodies were discovered three years ago, there have been calls for the government to impose tougher regulations on religious organisations. It also emerged that Mackenzie was arrested twice in the past, but then released.

articles.title: Russia to UAE, Iran steps up diplomacy amid Trump threats: What we know
articles.summary: Iran launches diplomatic offensive as US mulls resumption of war.
articles.body:
Iran has stepped up diplomatic efforts amid suggestions by United States President Donald Trump that the US could resume full-scale strikes on Iran.

The US news website Axios quoted a US official saying that US Central Command (CENTCOM) was preparing for the resumption of major military operations in Iran, and that it was just waiting on orders from Washington. On Thursday, Trump told reporters the US may have to “destroy” the rest of Iran, adding that people will “know soon enough” if he acts.

Tehran’s intensified diplomatic push comes after Iran downed two US reconnaissance drones near Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, which the US struck earlier this week. Iran says it will retaliate if the US resumes larger strikes.

What diplomatic efforts is Iran engaging in?

On Thursday, Iran offered the US a new nuclear and peace proposal via Qatari mediators, to be discussed only after Washington meets Tehran’s seven demands, a senior Iranian official told Reuters. The US is examining the proposal, Reuters reported.

Iran has made meeting its seven demands a condition for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and restarting peace talks, including on its nuclear programme. The demands include the lifting of sanctions on Iran, the unfreezing of Iranian assets and the end to the US naval blockade of its ports in and around the Strait of Hormuz, among other things.

It has also stepped up ties with Russia, with its top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, travelling to Moscow for talks on Thursday. During that visit, Rezaei said: “On the issue of diplomacy, we have announced seven conditions ⁠to the Americans. As long as they do ⁠not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations.”

Meanwhile, the US has insisted a deal on Iran’s nuclear capacity must be part of any ceasefire agreement before wider peace talks can restart.

On Thursday, Rezaei met with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin to deliver a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Iranian state media did not elaborate on ⁠the contents of the message.

Rezaei called it “an extremely important exchange” according to remarks reported by the Iranian embassy, but also did not give further details.

However, The Financial Times reported that Russia previously agreed to supply Iran with 90 helicopter-mounted launchers for precision-guided missiles, despite needing its own weapons for the Ukraine war. The newspaper cited a Russian defence manufacturer’s production schedule for 2024 and 2025, which it has examined, showing an order for helicopter-mounted launchers being assigned a code used to refer to Iran in Russian defence documents.

Relations between Russia and Iran have deepened since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and during the US-Israeli war on Iran that saw the two countries become the most heavily sanctioned in the world. Iran has provided Shahed drones, which Russia has modified and used heavily against Ukraine.

In return, Russia has also reportedly helped Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles, sold it Verba shoulder-launched anti-air missiles and shared information with Tehran potentially relevant to nuclear weapons.

“It is indicative of Russia’s willingness to continue supplying Iran despite its own wartime demands and with far less concern about Western objections than in the past,” Nicole Grajewski, a non-resident scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told the FT.

In early October, Putin said Russia was prepared to take part in mediation to bring an end to the war .

Images released by the Kremlin showed its foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov and chief of the Russian military intelligence, Igor Kostyukov, attending a meeting with Iran’s security chief alongside Putin.

The meeting also strengthened Iran’s economic ties with Russia.

“During the meeting with Mr Vladimir Putin, discussions were held regarding the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran,” said Rezaei, Iranian state TV reported.

He said the gas pipelines would address Iran’s gas shortages and facilitate the sale of Russian energy to neighbouring countries.

Tehran said Iran’s natural gas refineries had been hit during the most intense phase of US-Israeli strikes on Iran earlier this year, which lasted 40 days.

Separately, Russia’s Foreign Ministry advised citizens against travel to Iran “In light of the remaining risks of a new escalation around Iran”.

How is Iran negotiating with regional leaders?

During the most intense fighting of the war, Iran struck bases in Gulf countries hosting US military assets, as well as civil and energy facilities and infrastructure.

Senior Iranian officials have repeatedly warned that any state helping the US to target the Islamic republic will be a “legitimate target” should US attacks resume.

On Thursday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held phone calls with several Gulf leaders, including the foreign minister of the UAE, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

They discussed regional developments as well as diplomatic efforts for stability in the region, according to Araghchi’s Telegram channel.

Araghchi spoke with Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud about efforts to improve security and stability in the region, according to the Saudi foreign ministry.

Araghchi also discussed de-escalation efforts with the foreign ministers of Kuwait and Turkiye.

In a separate call, Araghchi talked with Qatar’s Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani about coordinating to reduce tensions, the Qatari foreign ministry said.

Sheikh Mohammed stressed support for efforts to secure freedom of maritime navigation.

In a statement, Oman’s foreign ministry said the safety of passage through the Strait of Hormuz was a main topic of discussions, in a call between Araghchi and Oman’s foreign minister.

Iran continues to tightly control shipping lanes through the strait, where several ships have been damaged in recent days. It has granted exemptions to shipping restrictions to Iraq and Qatar, in the Gulf region, as well as to India and China.

Despite his Republican Party suffering a drubbing in this week’s US midterm elections – largely because of public anger over the war on Iran and the resulting rise in energy prices – US President Donald Trump has refused to rule out further strikes on Iran.

On Thursday, Trump told reporters at the Oval Office that he may have to “destroy the rest” of Iran.

Former Iranian diplomat Hadi Afghahi told Al Jazeera that Tehran can ease the path to a settlement if the US also shows flexibility. He argued that Trump “really does not want to go to war, because war again will cost him more”. However, the US president’s next move is unpredictable, observers say.

Afghahi cautioned that Trump “is still surrounded by a group of hawks”, including the energy and treasury secretaries.

Trump has shown willingness to engage in diplomacy, however. Qatar’s ⁠Emir ⁠Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad ⁠Al Thani discussed diplomatic ⁠efforts to ease regional tensions in a ‌phone call with Trump on Friday, according to the Qatari Emiri Diwan.

The leaders reviewed international diplomatic efforts, including the Doha-led mediation efforts to support negotiations in recent weeks, in a bid to reach “a comprehensive agreement that puts an end to the crisis”, the Diwan said in a statement.

How has Iran responded to Trump’s rhetoric?

Tehran warned it will retaliate on a wider scale than it has done so far if the US resumes the war. It has also said talks will become unfeasible.

Iranian officials said Iran has the capacity to strike further than the Gulf using weapons manufactured in Iran.

On Thursday, a spokesman for the Supreme Advisor to the Commander of the Aerospace Force of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said: “In the event of a new aggression, any country or force that helps America attack Iran can be a legitimate target of the Islamic Republic.”

Iran’s state media outlet Tasnim News reported: “Our missile bases have a suitable range to target the Zionist regime and American bases,” adding “Iran’s response to the possible new aggression of the enemies will not be geographically limited.”

Iran has also previously warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence (AI) facilities across the Gulf region could be attacked if war with the US erupts again.

What strikes have there been in recent days?

In the run-up to the midterm elections, the US said it had conducted “defensive strikes” on Iran’s Qeshm Island and Bandar Lengeh in the Strait of Hormuz.

Meanwhile, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps navy says at least seven tankers have caught fire after sailing into mines while attempting to transit through the Strait of Hormuz using “unauthorised routes” near Oman this week.

Two oil ‌tankers caught fire and were brought to a stop after hitting ⁠mines on Friday, the IRGC said. They had been trying to cross the waterway “with the support of the aggressor and terrorist American military”, the IRGC added.

Control over the Strait of Hormuz has been a main stumbling block in negotiations to end the Iran war since it began in February.

Tehran has sought to limit traffic through the strategic waterway, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil supplies.

The US has also imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and escorted tankers through the strait.

Maritime organisations have not confirmed the latest incidents.

Russian President Vladimir Putin meets Iranian security council chief Mohsen Rezaei in Moscow, Russia, on November 5, 2026 [File: Pool via Reuters]

articles.title: Cannonballs unearthed at Alamo nearly 200 years after deadly siege, yet mystery remains
articles.summary: Solid cannonballs unearthed near Alamo Church mark the first such artifacts found at the historic San Antonio site in Texas from the 1836 battle. An expert spoke with Fox News Digital.
articles.body: Archaeologists in San Antonio, Texas, have announced the discovery of two solid cannonballs from the Battle of the Alamo — each offering new physical evidence of the historic battle. The discovery, made along the perimeter of Alamo Church in San Antonio, was announced in late October. Officials from the Alamo Trust said the cannonballs were uncovered during ongoing archaeological excavations at the site, and that they "help us remember those individuals that were living here, during the battle," said Tiffany Lindley, head archaeologist at the Alamo Trust. HIDDEN REVOLUTIONARY WAR BAKE HOUSE IS UNCOVERED AFTER SPENDING CENTURIES UNDERGROUND The solid-shot cannonballs vary in size, with the smaller measuring 1.8 inches in diameter and the larger measuring 3.26 inches. The measurements correspond to 1-pounder and 6-pounder cannons, respectively. The discovery follows two other finds made earlier this year: a 4-pounder cannonball found in March, on the eve of the battle's 190th anniversary, and a 6-pounder cannonball found in June. The total number of found cannonballs is now four. Photos show archaeologists carefully cleaning the newly discovered cannonballs, which appear heavily weathered and discolored. The Battle of the Alamo was one of the most important events in Texas history. EXPERTS FINALLY SOLVE MYSTERY OF TEENAGE REVOLUTIONARY WAR SOLDIER 246 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH The engagement lasted from Feb. 23 to March 6, 1836. It saw Texian forces — including Davy Crockett and William B. Travis — hold off a much larger Mexican army. The 13-day siege ended with Mexican troops overrunning the Texian defenders, a loss that became a rallying cry for the Texas Revolution. The discoveries raise a question: Which army fired the cannonballs? Lindley of the Alamo Trust told Fox News Digital the answer is a bit complicated. REVOLUTIONARY WAR ARTIFACTS UNEARTHED AT SITE OF INFAMOUS COLONIAL AMERICAN HEIST: 'VERY SURPRISED' "We have a good idea [of] three of the cannonballs … They were bronze cannonballs, and that was a type of material used by the Mexican army, so they may have originated with the Mexican army," she said. "They would have been shooting toward the church in this area." She noted, however, that the cannonballs could have been picked up by the Alamo's defenders or others before the battle, so either side may have used them. Determining whether the cannonballs were connected to the battle is more straightforward. Lindley said archaeologists can link the artifacts to the battle through several lines of evidence, including the layers of soil in which they were found, plus other objects recovered nearby. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The same soil deposit contained musket balls and gun parts, while its depth suggested the artifacts were older than others found in layers above it. Lindley said historians helped archaeologists determine that the cannonballs were likely found near a Mexican cannon position outside the Alamo. "They would have been shooting toward the church in this area," she said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Lindley, who said she was unaware of any solid cannonballs found at the site before the current project, attributed the recent discoveries largely to the size of the excavation area. For Lindley, the discovery also puts a tangible piece of the 1836 battle into the hands of modern-day archaeologists. articles.title: Lilly to sell obesity drugs directly on Hims & Hers site
articles.summary: Nov 6 (Reuters) - Eli Lilly said on Friday it struck a deal to allow Hims & Hers Health to sell obesity drugs Zepbound and Foundayo directly ‌on its platform...
articles.body:
FILE PHOTO: An injection pen of Zepbound, Eli Lilly’s weight loss drug, is displayed in New York

Nov 6 (Reuters) - Eli Lilly said on Friday it struck a deal to allow Hims & Hers Health to sell obesity drugs Zepbound and Foundayo directly ‌on its platform, sending the telehealth company's shares up more than 7% in premarket ‌trading.

The Lilly drugs were previously available to patients on Hims & Hers only if they left the site and went to ​Lilly's own cash-pay platform LillyDirect.

The move puts Lilly on equal footing with Danish rival Novo Nordisk, which has been selling its Wegovy and Ozempic through Hims & Hers since March, after previously suing the telehealth company for offering compounded versions of its medications.

Calling the Lilly partnership "a clear positive", Leerink Partners analyst ‌Michael Cherny said the deal completes ⁠Hims & Hers' process to secure access to the two leading GLP-1 drugmakers and should help provide broader access to branded weight-loss treatments following the company's ⁠exit from mass compounding.

Lilly leads the obesity drug market with its highly effective injectable Zepbound, even as Novo has sold millions more obesity pills in the US. Lilly launched its oral Foundayo in April, ​around three ​months after Novo's Wegovy pill came to market.

"The ease ​and ability for someone on the ‌Hims & Hers platform today to get Lilly medicine is not fully straightforward," said Ilya Yuffa, president of Lilly USA.

He said any friction point for consumers increases the chance of abandonment.

As part of the deal, Yuffa said Hims & Hers has agreed to not sell any compounded versions or knockoffs of Lilly's obesity medications.

Self-pay pricing starts at $149 per month for Lilly's obesity pill Foundayo and $299 per month ‌for injectable GLP-1 Zepbound, matching the prices available through ​LillyDirect.

Novo's drugs on the platform start at $149 per month ​for the Wegovy pill and $199 per month ​for the Wegovy injector pen.

Some 40% to 45% of Zepbound sales are ‌through self-pay channels, according to Lilly.

Analysts have said ​that Hims & Hers may ​get a boost next year from employers dropping coverage of weight-loss drugs to rein in costs.

Last week, Lilly raised its full-year revenue forecast by $5 billion on booming demand for ​its injectable weight-loss drugs. The company's ‌lead in the enormous and expanding obesity drug market has propelled Lilly to ​a $1.2 trillion market valuation.
