articles.title: ABC's 'The View' hosted just one conservative guest before Election Day, MRC study finds
articles.summary: ABC News' "The View" hosted just one conservative guest before Election Day this season, according to a Media Research Center study of its guest list.
articles.body: ABC News' "The View" hosted just one conservative guest and 21 liberal guests in the weeks leading up to Election Day, according to a new study by the conservative media watchdog Media Research Center (MRC). The study found that from Sept. 8, the start of Season 30, through Nov. 3, "The View" invited 21 liberal guests who were either critical of President Donald Trump or the Republican Party, with Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, being the lone conservative guest. Four of the guests classified as liberal were politicians: Gov. Andy Beshear, D-Ky.; Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz.; Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, who appeared on the show the day before Election Day alongside liberal podcast host Kara Swisher. Although a retiring Republican senator, Tillis was included in the liberal guest count due to being invited on to discuss his anti-Trump book, "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents." STEPHEN A SMITH DOUBLES DOWN ON TRUMP DINNER, CHALLENGES CRITICS BY ASKING, 'WHAT THE F--- ARE YOU DOING?' Tillis has been vocal in calling for Secretary of War Pete Hegseth's firing and has publicly broken with the president over the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill. In his book, Tillis wrote that he hoped Republicans would learn from midterm losses, which he predicted when the book was released in early October. "What I hope is that members of my party take the loss and learn something," he wrote, according to The New York Times, "specifically that putting party affiliation — or loyalty to one man — before your own conscience never turns out well in the end." The show hosted several liberal celebrities as well, including Maisie Williams, Ethan Hawke, Chelsea Handler, Michael Douglas, Billy Crystal, Patricia "Ms. Pat" Williams-Lee, D.L. Hughley, Chandra Wilson, Busy Philipps, Lin-Manuel Miranda, Eisa Davis, Jamie Lee Curtis and Sophia Bush. Neil deGrasse Tyson and Stephen A. Smith were among the other guests included in the study. Smith appeared on the show to discuss his recent White House meeting with Trump, a decision that drew criticism from the co-hosts. He defended his decision to attend. The ESPN host also criticized the president during the appearance. TRUMP SPILLS DETAILS ABOUT DINNER WITH BILL MAHER, STEPHEN A SMITH AND KID ROCK AT THE WHITE HOUSE According to the study's methodology, guests had to express liberal or conservative views during their appearances on the talk show to be counted in either category. "If a celebrity did not discuss politics, they were not included in the count of political leanings even if they had a history of being outspoken in the past," the MRC said. The show hosted 56 guests in total between Sept. 8 and Nov. 3, according to the study. The daytime talk show drew scrutiny in 2025 after hosting 128 liberal guests over the course of the year and just two conservatives. In 2026, the show hosted Vice President JD Vance and Alina Habba, a former legal spokesperson for Trump. The show also had several Republican fill-in co-hosts while Alyssa Farah Griffin was on maternity leave. The fill-ins included Elisabeth Hasselbeck and Savannah Chrisley, among others. In January 2026, the co-hosts interviewed former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, a Republican who became a fierce Trump critic. "The View" did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment. 'THE VIEW' CO-HOST WARNS AGAINST VANCE INTERVIEW BECOMING 'FREE-FOR-ALL' TO SELL BOOKS MRC President David Bozell said in a statement, "ABC has learned nothing from the FCC’s continued scrutiny. 'The View' continues to insult the intelligence of the American public by passing off pure Democratic propaganda as a ‘bona fide news program.’" "With 21 anti-Republican voices and a single conservative in the two months before the midterms, ABC’s political agenda could hardly be more obvious," he continued. "And ABC is hardly alone. The entire elitist media landscape deserves serious scrutiny. The Federal Communications Commission must hold ABC accountable for its abuse of the public airwaves for partisan political purposes." The program has faced a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) investigation over the past year. ABC has responded by defending "The View" as a "bona fide news" program. The investigation is related to the agency's crackdown on equal-time requirements for political candidates. A source at the FCC told Fox News Digital in February that the show's interview with James Talarico triggered the probe. "'The View' has been broadcasting under a bona fide news exemption granted to it more than twenty years ago ... The Commission has taken no action over the last two decades to modify or overturn the Declaratory Ruling and there is no basis for doing so now," ABC said in a petition in May in response to the FCC's probe. 'THE VIEW' EASED UP ON POLITICAL CANDIDATE BOOKINGS AMID FCC INQUIRY, REPORT SAYS The co-hosts interviewed Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico on Wednesday after he won his election in Texas and interviewed Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Thursday after his election victory. articles.title: Ukraine raises Zaporizhia aid strike death toll to at least 50
articles.summary: Ukrainian officials say DNA tests are being used to identify bodies while up to 39 remain trapped under rubble.
articles.body:
The death toll from a Russian attack on an aid distribution centre in Ukraine’s Zaporizhia region has risen to at least 50 people, making it one of the deadliest Russian attacks this year.

Ukraine’s emergency service announced on Friday that the toll from Monday’s strike on the village of Komyshuvakha has risen after eight more bodies were recovered from the rubble.

Acting regional governor Mykhailo Semikin later said that the death toll reached 53 people, as rescuers continued their search for missing bodies for the fifth day.

Al Jazeera was not able to independently verify that figure.

Local police on Wednesday said that 59 people were listed as missing, though some might be among the bodies already found.

“As many as 39 people may still remain trapped under the debris,” they said.

As rescuers continue to work, specialists have been taking DNA samples to identify the bodies. Continuing Russian attacks have also remained a constant threat to the rescue operation.

Ukraine said that Russian aircraft bombed a former school near the front lines on Monday, which civilians used for weekly aid handouts.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a second wave of bombs then hit the underground shelter where people had taken cover, causing most of the destruction.

“After the first aerial bomb strike, there was a double-tap strike with nine more bombs, specifically targeting the shelter where people were taking cover,” he said on X.

Four police officers and two rescue workers were also among the dead.

Zelenskyy called it a “vile terrorist strike” and said it signalled Moscow’s refusal to stop the fighting. The UN human rights mission in Ukraine also said the strike was likely a breach of international law.

The attack on Monday came only a day after a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky ended.

Russia and Ukraine both continued to trade drone attacks on Thursday, which injured several people on both sides, including a child.

On Wednesday, in the eastern Donetsk region, Russian attacks killed four civilians and injured five others.

Delegations from both Ukraine and Russia are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11 for US-brokered talks, though previous rounds made little progress.

articles.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production after years of poor sales in few markets
articles.summary: Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks that ultimately only sold in just a handful of markets because of its heavy, angular design.
articles.body: Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks that ultimately only sold in just a handful of markets because of its heavy, angular design. Musk said in an X post the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased output of its newly launched Cybercab model, which the billionaire has made central to Tesla's robotaxi ambitions. While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the model's specialized components. In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era." Tesla did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment sent outside regular business hours. The US EV maker only began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. Before the pickup truck launched, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units. "It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. "Every rational auto guy would say the same." "It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves." Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Its angular design was mocked by pickup truck purists and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe. The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them - only to leave massive cracks in two of them. During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future." But the vehicle has struggled to meet those expectations. Automotive analyst Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pick-ups from Ford and others have also flopped in the US market. "All of them lost the competition because electric pick ups aren't popular in the US," Munoz said. But Cybertruck's sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact. "Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said. The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk's key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an AI and robotics company rather than just an automaker. Musk has said he sees it as Tesla's main autonomous model supplying a global network of robotaxis. After years of delays to Musk's self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September. However, the automaker still has to answer the US auto safety agency's questions on whether it has properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards. "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab," Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

articles.title: Tehran thinks time is now on its side, but it has read the midterms wrong
articles.summary: Despite Iranian efforts to delay negotiations until a Democratic Congress takes office in January, the current administration faces mounting pressure to resolve the conflict due to domestic economic concerns and ongoing maritime tensions.
articles.body:
The Qatari mediators who spent more than 12 hours in Tehran at the end of October were racing against an American calendar. According to Axios , their aim was to get Iranian and American negotiators back into the same room before Americans went to the polls. Doha’s proposal was modest by design: phased, mutual steps over several days, followed by talks on the nuclear file, all while pressing Iran to let UN inspectors visit the facilities bombed during the war. The mediators spoke of progress.

Then the U.S. voted, and the arithmetic in Tehran changed almost overnight.

Seen from Iran, Tuesday’s result must look like relief arriving from an unexpected quarter . Democrats won both chambers , and the House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has listed ending the war among his four priorities. CNBC noted that the new majorities could push through a binding War Powers Resolution that would direct President Trump to stop unless Congress authorizes the conflict. Tehran’s foreign ministry had already said on the eve of the vote that the next move belonged to Trump, and that Iran’s core demands would not change. Every incentive now points toward waiting: slow-walk Doha, let the gavel change hands on Jan. 3, and negotiate later with a Washington that has two addresses instead of one.

There is a genuine logic behind this, and it should be acknowledged. Iran’s leadership has not forgotten 2018, when Trump walked out of a nuclear agreement that Tehran was complying with. Any settlement signed with him alone carries the same risk of being torn up overnight, and a deal in which a Democratic Congress has invested in, looks like a sturdier piece of paper. It seems a reasonable calculation. In practice, it rests on three misreadings of what the election actually changed.

The first misreading is legal. A Democratic-controlled Congress can pass a war powers resolution, but Trump can veto it, and overriding him needs two-thirds of both chambers. Democrats have won 54 Senate seats so far by the latest AP count , not 67. Even the outgoing Republican House passed a resolution to halt the war in June, when a handful of Republicans crossed over, and the bombing carried on regardless. Congress can starve a war of money, hold hearings and make the Pentagon’s life difficult. It cannot sign a ceasefire on Iran’s behalf, and it cannot lift a single sanction without a president’s cooperation.

The second misreading concerns the calendar. Between now and Jan. 3, the war runs entirely on Trump’s timetable, with a Republican Congress still in place to protect him. The Wall Street Journal reported that he told Gulf allies to prepare for a brief , high-intensity campaign after the election, and he has said more than once that the war would be put away one way or the other . A Tehran that is seen to be stalling hands him the justification he needs to use those nine weeks. Iran’s own belligerency at sea is supplying the rest. Its military said on Wednesday that four tankers burned after hitting mines near Hormuz, the latest in a string of incidents in waters American forces insist they have cleared. Every such claim strengthens the case for exactly the kind of escalation that Democrats will be powerless to prevent before January.

The third misreading is the most expensive, because it ignores where Trump himself now stands. He admitted to Fox that “a part of it was Iran.” A White House official spent election night predicting that Democratic voters would suffer “buyer’s remorse” once gas prices fall after the Iran conflict is solved, which is another way of saying that the administration’s political recovery now depends on a settlement. Brent crude sat at $104.36 a barrel on Wednesday morning. A president with two years left, a new majority vowing to drive out his Defense secretary and a party that blames him for the rout needs lower pump prices well before the 2028 primaries begin.

Israel, the other party to this imbroglio, is in no position to spoil a deal either. Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc finished with 53 seats in the Oct. 27 election, short of the 61 needed to govern, and coalition talks could drag on for weeks. A caretaker government in Jerusalem is poorly placed to wreck a ceasefire it did not negotiate.

Taken together, these factors give Tehran the strongest bargaining position it has held since February, and that position will not last. Iran’s economy is absorbing an American blockade of its ports , while the U.S. says it has helped Gulf states export 1.5 billion barrels through the strait since the summer. Those exports keep flowing whether or not Iran negotiates, and time is far less neutral than Tehran imagines.

The sensible course for Iran is the opposite of waiting. It should accept the phased proposal now, with a public deadline of mid-December, and let inspectors into at least one bombed site as the first visible step. Doha has already secured the essential concession from Washington, Trump’s agreement to keep pursuing talks at the request of Qatar, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states. An interim agreement concluded during the lame duck would arrive in January in front of a Democratic Congress with every political reason to protect it and none to sabotage it.

The durability problem that worries Tehran is real, and nothing guarantees a Trump signature for long. But a deal that a new congressional majority inherits and defends is the closest thing to a guarantee Iran is likely to see from Washington before 2029, and an agreement that is never signed offers no protection at all.

The test is a simple one. If Iranian negotiators are back in Doha before the end of November, Tehran will have read the election correctly. If they choose instead to wait for Speaker Jeffries, we must expect American aircraft to return to Iranian skies before he takes the gavel.

Imran Khalid is a physician and has a master’s degree in international relations.

articles.title: Zelensky: Ukraine may receive increased US assistance following ‘new political infrastructure’
articles.summary: The chances have increased for Ukraine to receive additional U.S. assistance, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday, reacting to Democrats’ overwhelming victories in the midterm elections. Ukraine needs to consolidate bipartisan support in the U.S. and “move toward” the new political infrastructure, he added in an interview with a Ukrainian news channel posted on the…
articles.body:
The chances have increased for Ukraine to receive additional U.S. assistance, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday, reacting to Democrats’ overwhelming victories in the midterm elections.

Ukraine needs to consolidate bipartisan support in the U.S. and “move toward” the new political infrastructure, he added in an interview with a Ukrainian news channel posted on the social platform X .

Zelensky said at least $16 billion in assistance was withheld by the U.S. and needs to be disbursed, and he said Ukraine needs a “package” from the U.S. to fortify itself in the face of ongoing Russian attacks. It was not immediately clear what funding Zelensky was referring to.

“We are grateful for everything that has been provided, but at the very least, Ukraine must fight for these funds,” he said.

Zelensky made the remarks on the sidelines of the Ibero-American Summit in Spain, where he said he secured a defense package from Spain worth $487 million. Germany has provided “a winter support package,” as Ukraine looks to build energy resilience against Russian attacks on its heating and electricity infrastructure.

The Ukrainian leader said he is also working to accelerate deliveries of missiles for Patriot air defense systems, other air-defense missiles and assistance for F-16 fighter jets.

Zelensky also said he had conversations with President Trump’s top envoys for negotiations, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, ahead of trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. scheduled in Abu Dhabi next week.

“The groundwork has been laid. It is important that everything is clear on paper. That there is an understanding of what the outcome will be,” Zelensky said in the interview.

“If Russia starts again, what will be done, by whom, with what means, and when? The answers should be clear first and foremost to us, Ukrainians. It is important for our society to know this.”

Republicans and Democrats who are supportive of Ukraine have raised the possibility of an aid package for the country over the next few weeks, with many of Kyiv’s most ardent GOP backers leaving Congress in January. Passing legislation before January could provide a majority to override a veto from Trump.

Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) told CBS News that additional assistance for Ukraine is a priority. And retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) has threatened to block the president’s agenda if additional Ukraine funding is not advanced. Democrats have pushed back on Trump’s attempt to import Russian diesel in violation of U.S. law.

Tankers carrying Russian diesel bound for the U.S. changed course following a letter from New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) warning port authorities they could face criminal or federal charges for unloading the oil, The Associated Press reported .

Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.), who lost his reelection race, had introduced legislation to nullify a waiver allowing the U.S. to import Russian diesel, enforce the existing ban and protect U.S. intelligence support for Ukraine, which has, at times, been halted under the Trump administration.

Still, a Democratic majority in both the House and Senate next Congress can earmark support for Ukraine in spending legislation. They are likely to prioritize shoring up Republican support for any spending bills to guard against a Trump veto during his lame-duck session.

articles.title: New bomb threats target European broadcasters, air traffic
articles.summary: A string of hoax alerts causing flight diversions across Europe this week has broadened to include newsrooms.
articles.body:
A new series of bomb threats caused more flight diversions across Europe on Friday, while also expanding to target a number of media organisations.

British broadcaster Sky said it was one of a number of newsrooms that received a bomb threat. “We have carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities,” a spokesperson said.

Bulgaria’s Nova TV and the Irish public broadcaster RTE received emailed bomb threats from a purported “Mikhail Andropov”, headlined “Message to the West”, portraying the threats as a prelude to more disruptions across Europe.

RTE briefly evacuated staff, including radio and television presenters, in Dublin after an email was received on Friday morning. RTE Radio One presenter David McCullagh later told listeners that the threat warned that a bomb would explode within 45 minutes.

The Irish government said hoax bomb claims were also sent to Virgin Media, Newstalk radio and The Irish Independent newspaper and that it was unclear who was behind them.

“However, these threats come on the heels of the ongoing disruption to aviation around Europe caused by similar threats, and it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption,” it said in a statement.

The incidents come a day after hoax bomb threats disrupted more than two dozen flights across Europe on Thursday, and days after other aircraft and a cruise ship received bomb alerts.

On Friday, jets escorted airliners flying from Brussels to Sofia and from Prague to Bucharest and Cyprus through Hungarian airspace due to bomb threats, Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said.

He also said NATO had ordered an air patrol near the Hungarian-Romanian border, the first report that the Western defence alliance had become involved.

Danish police said threats were directed at traffic at Copenhagen airport but that there appeared to be no danger to passengers. The airport said it was “operating normally”.

Czech police registered bomb threats to nine flights departing from or arriving in Prague. An airport spokesperson said no flights had been ⁠⁠cancelled as a result.

France said four new bomb threats were made to aircraft flying over French territory, and that all landed safely.

A Ryanair flight from Rome landed as scheduled in Lisbon, CNN Portugal reported.

About half a dozen ‌‌flights were disrupted on Tuesday and more than two dozen on Thursday, some of them making unplanned landings or being escorted to their destinations by fighter jets.

Al Jazeera’s Frances Read, reporting from London on Friday, said that while the threats have not been credible so far, disruptions appear to be widening .

“The number of hoax threats this week is making governments sit up and take notice about where this might be coming from and also think of solutions for how to deal with it,” she said.

articles.title: Netanyahu’s reign may not be over, but it should be
articles.summary: Another Netanyahu government would not bode well either for Israel or for the U.S.
articles.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may not have won a majority of Knesset seats in Israel’s latest election, but he has never done so. That has not prevented him from being Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.

Once again, he will try to stitch together a coalition of non-Arab parties, no matter how distasteful their leaders might be, in order to remain in power. Not coincidentally, success means that he can avoid facing the prospect of conviction in his long-running trial for corruption and bribery .

Netanyahu’s Likud party won a plurality of Knesset seats but fell short of its current representation in the parliament. On the other hand, the opposition coalition, led by former Israeli Defense Force chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, won a larger plurality, although his own party won fewer seats than Likud. Unless Eisenkot can demonstrate that his coalition could garner a majority of 61 seats, Israeli President Isaac Herzog may have little choice but to ask Netanyahu to attempt to form a new government.

Another Netanyahu government would not bode well either for Israel or for the U.S. The Israeli leader has been pushing President Trump to launch another aerial assault on Iran. Netanyahu did so prior to the election , presumably hoping that, were Israel engaged in operations against the Tehran regime, Israeli voters would rally round his leadership. That did not happen.

Once the elections were over, but prior to the American congressional elections, Netanyahu, now a caretaker prime minister, in what was termed a “candid” conversation between the two leaders, Trump again rebuffed Netanyahu. With the American elections over, Trump is now facing the prospect of a far more hostile Congress that likely will throttle his legislative initiatives and perhaps even his political appointments. Trump will therefore devote most of his attention to foreign affairs, where he would have greater freedom from Congressional restraint and may then be more inclined to accede to Netanyahu’s urgent pleas.

Should Eisenkot successfully put together a governing coalition, he is unlikely to pressure Trump as Netanyahu has done. The challenge Eisenkot faces, however, is how to cobble together a government without including the Arab parties that together won 19 seats and thus became the key to any outright government majority.

Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, publicly opposes including Arab parties in his government; only three Israeli Arabs (one of them Druze) have ever served as Israeli ministers since Israel’s independence in 1948. Unlike Netanyahu, however, Eisenkot appears to be somewhat more flexible on this issue. Whereas Netanyahu might be comfortable with a deadlocked Knesset that would prompt him to call for another election, Eisenkot recognizes that, like many who led the opposition to the wily prime minister in previous elections, he may have no second chance if he fails.

Former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman has announced that he will not serve in a government that includes Israeli Arabs. Eisenkot must therefore weigh whether he is prepared to include one more more of the Arab parties in his government while cajoling Lieberman to reverse his stance.

Eisenkot has three options that could enable him to form a government. Netanyahu has called for a “national unity” government that would allow him to remain prime minister. It is unlikely that Eisenkot would agree to such an arrangement, which could leave him sidelined, even if he is a government minister. Alternatively, he could reach an agreement with the Arab parties to support his minority government, in exchange for a variety of concessions such as directing more government resources to support currently underfunded programs to support the living conditions of Israel’s Arab citizens. Finally, he could offer Ra’am party leader Mansour Abbas in particular a job as either deputy minister (perhaps for foreign affairs) or director general of the Foreign Ministry. Doing so would win Ra’am’s support and likely further undergird Israel’s ties with the Gulf Arab states.

There is a precedent for such an arrangement. For years, Israel’s ultra-orthodox religious parties stated that they refused to take ministerial posts in any Israeli government (they have since done so). On the other hand, they were prepared to, and did, fill deputy ministerships during that period. Such an arrangement, this time with Arab deputy ministerships, might sufficiently mollify Liberman to make him agree to join an Eisenkot-led government.

Netanyahu may have overtaken David Ben Gurion’s record as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, but in recent years he has seriously damaged Israel’s international standing. He has also exhausted his military with multi-front wars and overseen a dual-track economy that has undermined the standard of living and purchasing power of the majority of his country’s population. His departure would not be missed, not only by many (and perhaps most) Israelis, but also by many Americans, including a majority of Jewish Americans.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

articles.title: Bengaluru gets dementia village offering free residential care to 100 elders
articles.summary: Bengaluru opens Smriti Gram, a free 100-bed dementia village by Nightingales Medical Trust, offering residential care, training and research for low-income elders.
articles.body: Bengaluru: According to experts, dementia care can cost anywhere between Rs 30,000 and Rs 1 lakh a month. Unable to afford these expenses, many families struggle to provide long-term care for elders with dementia, leaving some vulnerable to neglect and abandonment. In an effort to address this gap, Smriti Gram, an integrated dementia village offering free residential care to 100 elders, was inaugurated Friday at Thirumagondanahalli near Doddaballapur, on the outskirts of Bengaluru.The 100-bed facility has been established by Nightingales Medical Trust (NMT), a non-profit organisation that works for senior citizens. It will provide free residential care exclusively to elders with dementia from economically disadvantaged and vulnerable backgrounds.The campus brings together specialised residential care, caregiver training, research and innovation under one roof. It will also serve as a centre for caregiver training and capacity building, with the aim of developing a skilled workforce for dementia and eldercare.NMT representatives said the initiative would explore the appropriate integration of evidence-based Indian systems of medicine with contemporary medical care, in collaboration with the Central Ayurveda Research Institute under the ministry of Ayush.“Our aspiration is to develop Smriti Gram into a sustainable model of integrated dementia care that can be replicated in different parts of the country,” said S Premkumar Raja, secretary, NMT. The long-term vision is to develop the campus into a 300-bed facility.The first phase, supported by donors, including the Azim Premji Foundation, will accommodate 100 elders.Besides residential wards, the campus has a memory wall featuring photographs depicting different stages of life, a prayer hall, a gaming area for cognitive activities and green spaces for walking. Residents will follow a structured daily schedule that will also include a “family-style social time.”Priority will be given to elders aged 55 years and above with a confirmed diagnosis of dementia, who require round-the-clock care and have little or no caregiver support. The free facility is intended for families whose annual income is below Rs 5 lakh.Dr Radha S Murthy, managing trustee, NMT, said, “There are many elders with dementia who are vulnerable, neglected, living alone or unable to receive the care they need because of financial and family circumstances. We want every elder who comes to Smriti Gram to feel safe, cared for and respected, and to live with dignity and security.”The facility was inaugurated by Lakshmi, one of the first residents of the facility.For admission enquiries: 080 4242 6565You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: Why is Denmark separating ‘Western’ and ‘non-Western’ citizens?
articles.summary: Evicted families take Denmark’s controversial ‘ghetto law’ to the Supreme Court.
articles.body:
Seven families from Helsingor, a coastal city north of Copenhagen, are facing their former landlord in Denmark’s Supreme Court.

In a two-day hearing that began on Friday, they are arguing they were forced from their homes because of where they, or their parents, come from.

Their leases were terminated in 2022 under a 2018 law, once known as the “ ghetto law ”, which targets social housing estates where more than half of residents are classed as “non-Western”. The government claims the law is aimed at integration. But rights groups have for years fought against the measures, saying they are discriminatory.

“It’s about whether the criteria regarding the tenants’ origin is neutral or not,” Eddie Khawaja, the families’ lawyer, told the news agency AFP.

So what does “non-Western” mean, and could the courts bring the law down? Here’s what you need to know:

It is a statistical label that covers most of the world.

In 2020, the UN Human Rights Office said: “Statistics Denmark, under the Danish Ministry for Economic and Interior Affairs, defines ‘non-Western’ as any country outside the EU, with the exceptions of Andorra, Australia, Canada, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, New Zealand, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the USA, and the Vatican State.

“The effect is that ‘non-Western’ disproportionately means Denmark’s non-white, non-European ethnic populations,” it stated. The label also covers descendants: anyone born in Denmark if neither parent is a Danish citizen born in the country.

That means a Danish citizen born and raised in Copenhagen can still be “non-Western”.

Every December 1, the government names “parallel societies”.

These are social housing areas of at least 1,000 people where more than 50 percent are “non-Western” immigrants and descendants.

An area must also meet two of four criteria on unemployment, crime, education, and income.

Areas on the list for five years become “transformation areas”, which the government used to call “hard ghettos”.

They must cut public family housing to 40 percent by 2030 through sales, demolition or conversion.

An estate with the same social problems but fewer “non-Western” residents faces no such obligation.

The government says the goal is integration.

The law was part of a plan called “One Denmark without Parallel Societies: No Ghettos in 2030”.

In 2021, Kaare Dybvad Bek, then interior minister, said too many non-Western foreigners in one area “increases the risk of an emergence of religious and cultural parallel societies”.

About 11,000 people across Denmark will have to leave their homes by 2030, according to tenants’ associations.

In Helsingor, the landlord Boliggarden announced in early 2020 that it would renovate 96 apartments at the Nojsomhed estate. It then terminated the tenants’ leases. Most of those tenants were of foreign origin.

“They didn’t want the estate to be labelled ‘hard ghetto’ so they wanted to forcibly move us out when we advocated for other solutions,” Riad, a 33-year-old plaintiff who did not want his family name published, told AFP.

The law may be discriminatory, but Danish judges ultimately make the final decision about whether it violated Danish laws prohibiting ethnic discrimination.

The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) ruled in December 2025, in cases brought by tenants from Mjolnerparken in Copenhagen and Schackenborgvaenge in Slagelse. It said nationality or country of birth alone does not determine ethnic origin, but an allegedly neutral criterion covering many origins could be linked to ethnicity.

That runs contrary to the Danish government’s position and the reasoning of the lower Danish courts in the Helsingor case, which found that the “non-Western” does not describe an ethnic group and therefore did not result in discrimination that violated Denmark’s Equal Treatment Act.

Danish judges must decide whether the “non-Western” criterion really rests on residents’ ethnic origin, the court said, and consequently, if people included in the criterion are afforded less favourable treatment.

Less favourable treatment, it noted, could include “an increased risk of early termination of their leases”.

In January, Sophie Haestorp Andersen, then minister for social affairs and housing, told a parliamentary hearing that authorities must keep applying the law until the Eastern High Court rules, the Danish outlet Danske Kommuner reported.

The four-party coalition in power since June includes the Green Left (SF), which voted for the law in 2018, according to the public broadcaster DR. The party’s Jacob Mark is now minister for children, elderly affairs and housing.

No date has been officially set for the verdict, but reports suggest it could be handed down later this month.

If the families win, they would probably be rehoused in homes similar to the ones they had to leave.

The Mjolnerparken case is still before the Eastern High Court.

articles.title: In 2014, Dean Norris paid $1.725 million for an 11-acre California ranch; 12 years later, the Breaking Bad star is asking $3.2 million as he faces divorce proceedings and his restaurant seeks bankruptcy protection
articles.summary: Dean Norris, best known as Hank Schrader on 'Breaking Bad', has listed his 11-acre Temecula ranch for $3,199,267 as he and his wife Bridget navigate
articles.body: Dean Norris, best known as Hank Schrader on 'Breaking Bad', has listed his 11-acre Temecula ranch for $3,199,267 as he and his wife Bridget navigate divorce proceedings and a bankruptcy filing involving their longtime restaurant. The actor bought the property in 2014 for $1.725 million, and the new asking price represents an increase of nearly $1.5 million over that original purchase, according to Page Six and TMZ.The sale comes at a complicated moment for the Norris family. Bridget filed for divorce in February 2025, citing irreconcilable differences, while the couple’s Temecula restaurant, Swing Inn Cafe, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September. The ranch listing, represented by Sherrie Snyder of Allison James Estates and Homes, offers a glimpse into the scale of the property the couple built together over more than a decade.A 7,000-square-foot estateThe Temecula estate spans about 7,000 square feet of living space and includes nine bedrooms and nine bathrooms. It also comes with a guesthouse, giving the property room for extended family, visitors or staff.Outdoor features are central to the listing. The ranch includes an infinity pool, spa, outdoor areas, a four-stall horse barn and a fruit orchard, making it as much a working property as a private residence.The 11-acre setting gives the home a rural feel while keeping it within reach of Temecula’s wine country and Southern California amenities. For a buyer seeking acreage, equestrian facilities and a large main house, the listing offers a combination that is increasingly rare in the region.What Norris paid in 2014Dean and Bridget Norris acquired the property in 2014 for $1,725,000. Page Six reports that the couple invested that amount when they bought the home, which they shared during much of their marriage.The current asking price of $3,199,267 is about $1.47 million higher than the 2014 purchase price. That represents an increase of roughly 85 percent, although the final sale price will depend on the market, negotiations and the condition of the property at closing.The listing has not yet produced a reported sale. What is clear is that Norris is seeking a substantial return on a property he has owned for 12 years, even as personal and business finances have become more complicated.A marriage ending in courtDean and Bridget Norris married on October 27, 2001, according to court documents obtained by TMZ. They share five children, including two minors, 17-year-old Zoe and 16-year-old Dean Jr.Bridget filed for divorce in Riverside County in February 2025, citing irreconcilable differences. She listed January 15, 2025 as the separation date and asked for joint legal and physical custody of the children, along with spousal support. She also asked the court to determine the couple’s rights to property acquired during the marriage. Dean responded to the filing months later, but the case does not appear to have been finalised.The Swing Inn Cafe bankruptcyThe financial pressure extends beyond the family home. Dean and Bridget purchased the Swing Inn Cafe in Temecula in 2022, taking over management of a business that has operated since 1927. The restaurant filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in September. Chapter 11 allows a business to reorganise its debts while continuing to operate, rather than immediately shutting down. According to documents obtained by Page Six, the business reported assets of $147,809.58 against liabilities of $1,811,598.46. TMZ reported that gross revenue fell by about $1 million from 2024 to 2025, which the company attributed in part to fading social media attention.Why the ranch sale mattersThe Temecula ranch is one of the couple’s most visible assets, and its listing comes as both the divorce and bankruptcy cases remain unresolved. Selling a property during a divorce can be part of a broader effort to divide assets, pay debts or simplify a complicated financial picture. For Norris, the ranch represents both a personal history and a potential source of liquidity. The property has been part of the family’s life for 12 years, but its sale could help address the financial pressures surrounding the Swing Inn Cafe and the ongoing divorce.The asking price reflects the scale of the estate rather than a guaranteed outcome. A 7,000-square-foot home with nine bedrooms, a guesthouse, horse barn, orchard and infinity pool will appeal to a specific kind of buyer, particularly one seeking acreage in Temecula.A career beyond 'Breaking Bad'Norris is best known for playing DEA agent Hank Schrader on AMC’s 'Breaking Bad', a role that made him a familiar face to television audiences worldwide. But his life in Temecula has involved more than acting.In addition to the Swing Inn Cafe, Dean and Bridget manage the Norris Performing Arts Center. Those ventures show a family that has invested in local businesses and community institutions, even as the restaurant now faces bankruptcy proceedings.The ranch listing, the divorce filing and the bankruptcy case together paint a picture of a public figure dealing with private financial strain. For now, the $3.2 million asking price is the most visible sign of that transition.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
